Multicalibration Boosting: Theory, Convergence, and Transferability

\nameHanxuan Ye \emailhanxuan.ye@pennmedicine.upenn.edu Affiliation: \addrDepartment of Biostatistics and Epidemiology Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Affiliation: Philadelphia, PA 19104-6021, USA    \nameHongzhe Li \emailhongzhe@pennmedicine.upenn.edu Affiliation: \addrDepartment of Biostatistics and Epidemiology Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Affiliation: Philadelphia, PA 19104-6021, USA
Abstract

Multicalibration extends classical calibration by requiring predictions to be unbiased over a rich collection of functions, encompassing both prediction slices and subpopulations. It has emerged as a powerful framework for fairness, robustness, and reliable prediction, yet the theoretical understanding of multicalibration boosting (MCBoost) remains fragmented and often relies on restrictive assumptions. In this work, we develop a unified and refined perspective on MCBoost that subsumes existing variants, including multiaccuracy, BatchGCP, and BatchMVP. We uncover several phenomena that provide new insights into its practical behavior: even highly accurate and flexible predictors can remain substantially miscalibrated; enforcing multicalibration introduces a calibration–risk trade-off; and early stopping plays a central role in controlling this trade-off. On the theoretical side, we establish a general framework for MCBoost under weaker and more realistic conditions. We show that the boosting iterates converge to a Bregman projection of the population-optimal predictor onto the cumulative span generated by the audit class, thereby explicitly characterizing the function space on which multicalibration is achieved. We further derive convergence rates under different smoothness assumptions, finite-sample guarantees, and principled stopping rules that ensure multicalibration at termination. Finally, we extend the theory of universal adaptability under covariate shift, providing more general transfer guarantees and clarifying when multicalibrated predictors generalize across domains. These results provide a more complete theoretical foundation and practical guidance for multicalibration boosting, positioning it as both a unifying framework and a reliable post-processing approach for modern predictive models.

Keywords: algorithm auditing; boosting; convex analysis; distribution shift; early stopping; fairness

1 Introduction

Multicalibration, introduced by Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018), asks a predictor to be unbiased not only marginally but also after conditioning on both predicted values and subgroup membership. It therefore strengthens classical calibration, which is already regarded as a central property of probabilistic prediction (Dawid, 1982; Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017). In the simplest binary-outcome setting, calibration requires that among units with predicted value vv, the average outcome is also vv; multicalibration extends this requirement to a rich family of subpopulations and prediction slices.

Since its introduction, the notion has broadened substantially. Jung et al. (2021) extended multicalibration to real-valued outcomes and higher moments. Gupta et al. (2021) developed online and quantile-oriented variants for uncertainty prediction, while Bastani et al. (2022); Jung et al. (2021) studied practical quantile calibration with connections to conditional coverage. A particularly useful unification is due to Deng et al. (2023), who replaced the residual f⁡(X)−Yf(X)-Y by a general score function s⁡(Y,f)s(Y,f) and thus encompassed a wide range of objectives, from fair uncertainty quantification to fairness constraints such as false-positive rate parity. More recently, the framework has been extended to the settings of vector-valued prediction (Zhang et al., 2024).

Beyond fairness, multicalibration has also emerged as a tool for robust learning under data heterogeneity. When training and test distributions differ but remain structurally related, post hoc multicalibration can yield predictors that adapt to new domains without retraining (Kim et al., 2022). This target-independent perspective connects multicalibration to domain adaptation and transfer learning. Empirically, boosting-based multicalibration has shown robust behavior across applications ranging from Gender Shades and Adult Income prediction (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018; Kim et al., 2019) to epidemiological studies such as NHANES and NHIS (Kim et al., 2022); see also Ye and Li (2025) for a survival-analysis extension based on pseudo-observations.

The practical appeal of multicalibration boosting (MCBoost) is clear: it can refine a pre-trained black box predictor through post-processing, regardless of whether it is well-trained or inadvertently chosen; it offers a route to target-independent adaptation when the relevant shifts lie near the learned calibration class, thus achieving universal adaptability (Kim et al., 2022); and it is especially attractive in multi-target settings where measuring demographic variables, estimating propensity scores are costly, or repeated access to raw data is difficult due to privacy constraints.

Despite rapid progress in both theory and applications, several core questions remain open. First, existing multicalibration algorithms are often developed for specific settings, and a unified algorithmic treatment remains relatively limited. While Deng et al. (2023) provided a broad infinite-sample analysis, their framework implicitly assumes a black-box optimization oracle and complete knowledge of the underlying distribution, as also discussed by Gibbs et al. (2025). Their algorithm is presented as a high-level sketch where parameter choice, sample complexity, and explicit sample-based auditing procedures are not the main focus. Second, the role of weak learners is not yet well understood: the auditing class clearly shapes the updates, but its effect on the limiting predictor and on the ultimate multicalibrated class has not been characterized systematically. Third, finite-sample guarantees could be improved, especially for convergence rates under varying smoothness and for the stopping rules used in practice. Although some studies provide upper bounds on the number of boosting iterations (Globus-Harris et al., 2023), a sharper characterization of convergence rates, sample complexity, and the effects of loss smoothness remains lacking. The theoretical justification for the practical stopping criterion, which underpins empirical success, has received limited attention. Finally, although multicalibration has been linked to target-independent learning (Kim et al., 2022), the precise scope of its guarantees under covariate shift deserves a more general treatment.

1.1 This paper

Motivated by these questions, we develop a unified framework for understanding multicalibration boosting across objectives such as squared loss and pinball loss. Our main contributions are as follows.

  • I

    Unified formulation of MCBoost. We propose a generalized multicalibration boosting procedure that subsumes the main variants in the literature, including standard calibration (Roth, 2022), multiaccuracy (Kim et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2022), BatchGCP (Jung et al., 2022), and BatchMVP (Jung et al., 2022) for equalized coverage.

  • II

    Limit characterization and the multicalibrated function class. Using convex analysis and Bregman geometry (Bauschke et al., 1997; Bauschke and Combettes, 2020), we show that the MCBoost limit is the Bregman projection of the population-optimal predictor onto the cumulative boosting span generated by the audit class, extending the classical L2L_{2}-projection interpretation known for regression with squared loss. More importantly, this yields an explicit characterization of the function class on which the final predictor is multicalibrated, in contrast to prior analyzes that treated the resulting multicalibrated class as implicit or left it unspecific using an agnostic argument. In general, it is the closure of the cumulative boosting span, which could be substantially richer than the original audit class. We view this identification as a central contribution, because it clarifies what MCBoost can ultimately calibrate and how the choice of auditor shapes the learned predictor.

  • III

    Convergence, finite-sample guarantees, and stopping. We derive explicit convergence rates for the excess risk under different smoothness regimes: sublinear under cLc_{L}-smoothness and geometric convergence under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. We also establish finite-sample guarantees, including sample-complexity bounds and an upper bound on the number of iterations before termination. The stopping rule used in practical implementations is shown to guaranty multicalibration once the algorithm halts, providing a principled explanation for the validity of practical implementations. The analysis also covers optional projections under milder and more realistic conditions than assumed in prior work (Deng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024), which are relevant for constrained predictors such as those taking values in [0,1][0,1].

  • IV

    Adaptation under covariate shift. We extend the theory of universal adaptability (Kim et al., 2022) under weaker assumptions and obtain more general guarantees. In particular, we provide refined bounds for target-domain error after multicalibration, characterize the transfer of multicalibration from source to nearby target distributions, and extend the framework to multi-source settings. These results clarify when multicalibration improves performance under distribution shift and highlight that its effectiveness depends on how well the relevant density ratios are represented within the learned learned function class.

This work provides a comprehensive theoretical treatment of multicalibration, unifying existing variants under a single boosting-based framework and rigorously identifying their limit behavior, convergence properties, and transferability.

Our numerical study is designed to illustrate practical implications of these ideas. The motivating simulation in Figure 1 shows that better global predictive accuracy does not necessarily imply smaller subgroup bias. The early-stopping experiments in Figures 2 and 3 provide qualitative evidence for the calibration-risk trade-off and the role of early stopping in controlling overfitting. The comparisons among various auditors give a practical sense of how auditor choice, group structure, and feature information affect MCBoost. The covariate-shift experiments likewise illustrate when performance can improve under structured shifts.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the generalized MCBoost framework and presents a motivating simulation that illustrates why calibration and accuracy do not necessarily coincide. Section 3 develops the main theory, including the limit characterization, the explicit multicalibrated class, convergence and finite-sample guarantees, stopping, and target-independent learning under dsitribution shift. Section 4 then studies auditor expressivity, group information, and structured shifts more in practice. Supplementary material contains proofs, additional examples, and additional numerical results.

1.2 Related work

Beyond the papers most directly aligned with ours, multicalibration has found use in several related areas. It has been used to promote fairness in ranking systems (Dwork et al., 2019), to give an indistinguishability-based interpretation of individual probabilities for non-repeatable events (Dwork et al., 2021), and to extend calibration ideas to censored survival outcomes (Ye and Li, 2025). The concept is also closely tied to omniprediction (Gopalan et al., 2021), which shows that sufficiently multicalibrated predictors can be transformed to perform nearly optimally across a large collection of downstream losses. Recent work has also begun to transport multicalibration ideas into modern applications. For example, Detommaso et al. (2024) proposed multicalibration-based hallucination scores for large language models using groups induced by embedding clusters or LLM-generated annotations. Related work on conditional coverage in conformal prediction (Romano et al., 2020a; Gibbs et al., 2025) shares similar goals with multicalibration approaches for equalized quantile coverage (Bastani et al., 2022; Jung et al., 2022), underscoring the broader connection between calibration, fairness, and reliable uncertainty quantification. On the algorithmic side, our work is also connected to the classical boosting literature (Freund and Schapire, 1997). Closely related are the function-space analysis of Bühlmann and Yu (2003) and Zhang and Yu (2005), which highlights early stopping as a way to control overfitting.

2 Multicalibration and the MCBoost framework

We study multicalibration as a general optimization-driven property of a predictor f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} relative to a score function s⁡(Y,u)s(Y,u), which often arises as a gradient or subgradient of a loss L⁡(Y,u)L(Y,u) with respect to its prediction argument uu. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a class of measurable functions, possibly depending on both covariates and predictions.

Definition 1

For tolerance α>0\alpha>0, a predictor ff is α\alpha-multicalibrated over ℋ\mathcal{H} if

suph∈ℋ|𝔼⁡[h⁡(X,f⁡(X))⋅s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))]|<α.\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\big|\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(X,f(X))\cdot s(Y,f(X))\right]\big|<\alpha. (1)

This more general notion can characterize functions obtained from various settings, such as: (i) regression and classification with squared loss L⁡(Y,f)=(Y−f)2/2L(Y,f)=(Y-f)^{2}/2; (ii) classification with logistic loss L⁡(Y,f)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−f​Y))L(Y,f)=\log(1+\exp(-fY)) or exponential loss L⁡(Y,f)=exp⁡(−f​Y)L(Y,f)=\exp(-fY); and (iii) quantile regression with pinball loss. The function hh can encode the group structure (e.g., h(X,f)=𝟏{X∈G}h(X,f)={\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}), value buckets (e.g., h(X,f)=𝟏{f∈I}h(X,f)={\mathbf{1}}\{f\in I\} for some value range II), or interactions h⁡(X,f)=𝟏​{X∈G,f∈I}h(X,f)={\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G,f\in I\}. In all cases, multicalibration asks that s⁡(Y,u)s(Y,u) have vanishing correlation, uniformly over ℋ\mathcal{H}.

A generic way to achieve multicalibration is the boosting scheme. We use boosting to reduce violations 𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))⋅h]\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f(X))\cdot h] over h∈ℋaudh\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} for some auditing class ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}. We summarize a generic version in Algorithm 1; it encompasses earlier variants for classification (Kim et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2022), as well as regression and quantile calibration (Jung et al., 2022). Basically, at each iteration, the algorithm (i) audits the current predictor f(b)f^{(b)}, (ii) selects the most violated direction h(b)∈ℋaudh^{(b)}\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} via an auditing oracle 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and (iii) updates f(b)f^{(b)} in the opposite direction of violation.

In Algorithm 1, the auditing procedure 𝒜\mathcal{A} determines the admissible form of hh. For instance, (i) a linear or Ridge regression could lead to h=X⊤β𝟏{f(b)(X)∈I}h=X^{\top}\beta{\mathbf{1}}\{f^{(b)}(X)\in I\}, representing a local linear correction within a funciton value range; (ii) Groupwise constant fit gives h=βG𝟏{X∈G}h=\beta_{G}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}, corresponding to subgroup refinements; (iii) tree-based or kernel regressors that fit s⁡(Y,f(b)​(Xi))s(Y,f^{(b)}(X_{i})) over partitioned regions of (X,f(b)​(X))(X,f^{(b)}(X)) space. The coefficients (e.g., β,βG\beta,\beta_{G}) are learned by 𝒜\mathcal{A} using data Ξ\Xi. The optional projection operator 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O} enforces a function within some closed space OO, e.g. O=𝒴=[0,1]O=\mathcal{Y}=[0,1].

2.1 A motivating simulation: accuracy is not enough

To motivate why MCBoost can still be useful even when a predictor already achieves good overall accuracy, we work with the numerical design used throughout the paper. We generate responses according to

Y=f1​(X(c))+f2​(X(d))+ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​(X(c),X(d))),Y=f_{1}(X^{(c)})+f_{2}(X^{(d)})+\varepsilon,\quad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}(X^{(c)},X^{(d)})),

where the covariates are partitioned into continuous and categorical components. Specifically, X(c)=(X1,…,X5)∼𝒩⁡(0,I5)X^{(c)}=(X_{1},\dots,X_{5})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{5}) and X(d)=(X6,X7)∈{0,1}2X^{(d)}=(X_{6},X_{7})\in\{0,1\}^{2}. Here, for illustrative purposes, let X6X_{6} represent gender (male=1, female=0), and X7X_{7} represent ethnicity (black=1, white=0). The heteroskedastic noise level is σ⁡(X(c),X(d))=σ⁡(1+0.2​X1+0.3​X6+0.25​X7),σ=0.5,\sigma(X^{(c)},X^{(d)})=\sigma\,(1+0.2X_{1}+0.3X_{6}+0.25X_{7}),\sigma=0.5, and the regression functions are

f1​(X(c))=X(c)⊤​β+0.8​sin⁡(X1)−0.5​(X22−1)+0.4​X1​X2,β=(1.2,0.9,0.6,0.4,0.2),f_{1}(X^{(c)})=X^{(c)\top}\beta+0.8\sin(X_{1})-0.5(X_{2}^{2}-1)+0.4X_{1}X_{2},\quad\beta=(1.2,0.9,0.6,0.4,0.2),

and

f2​(X(d))=−0.7​X6+0.8​X7+0.4​X6​X7.f_{2}(X^{(d)})=-0.7X_{6}+0.8X_{7}+0.4X_{6}X_{7}.

This design separates global predictive accuracy from subgroup bias. Standard criteria such as MSE or MAE quantify pointwise accuracy, whereas multicalibration asks whether residual bias remains after conditioning on subgroups and prediction levels. Consequently, a method looks strong under global loss may still exhibits substantial subgroup-level discrepancies.

That is exactly what Figure 1 shows. Flexible models such as random forests often achieve lower MSE, yet they need not exhibit smaller subgroup bias than a simpler linear model. By contrast, a linear model can satisfy global moment conditions such as

X⊤​(𝐲−𝐟^)=0,X^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\widehat{\mathbf{f}})=0,

which enforce calibration along the observed linear features, including group indicators when those features are included. But real groups are often nonlinear, intersected, or prediction-dependent. MCBoost is therefore best viewed as a post-processing layer that retains a good initial fit while explicitly targeting the remaining structured biases.

2.2 Specialization and prior algorithms as instances

To get better understanding of the abstract or formalized languaged Algorithm 1, we highlight that it includes the procedure of earlier work by Kim et al. (2019); Kim et al. (2022), which is modified slightly and is presented in Algorithm 2. Their audited learner depends solely on covariates h=h⁡(X)h=h(X), but the algorithm effectively incorporates prediction buckets by conditioning on value ranges of f(b)​(X)f^{(b)}(X). Each bucket {X∈Sl}\{X\in S_{l}\} corresponding to multiplying h⁡(X)h(X) by an indicator 𝟏{X∈Sl}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in S_{l}\}, thus implicitly creating functions of the form h(X)𝟏{f(b)(X)∈Il}h(X){\mathbf{1}}\{f^{(b)}(X)\in I_{l}\}. More recent formulations (Deng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024) makes this structure explicit by allowing the auditor to depend jointly on covariates and predictions, making h=h⁡(X,f⁡(X))h=h(X,f(X)), as in (1). This broader perspective requires the score function s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))s(Y,f(X)) to be unbiased not only within subpopulations defined by XX, but also conditional on the predicted value f⁡(X)f(X) itself, thereby extending the classical calibration.

A convenient and widely used construction takes the tensor-product form

ℋaud={h(X,f)=h1(X)h2(f(X)):h1∈ℋX,h2∈ℋf}=ℋX⊗ℋf,\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{h(X,f)=h_{1}(X)h_{2}(f(X)):h_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{X},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H}_{f}\}=\mathcal{H}_{X}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{f}, (4)

Here ℋX\mathcal{H}_{X} captures the partition of the covariate space, e.g., ℋX={βG𝟏{X∈G}:G∈𝒢}\mathcal{H}_{X}=\{\beta_{G}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}:G\in\mathcal{G}\} or ℋX={h(X)𝟏{X∈G}:G∈𝒢}\mathcal{H}_{X}=\{h(X){\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}:G\in\mathcal{G}\} for tree-based h⁡(X)h(X). The class ℋf\mathcal{H}_{f} stratifies the sample according to the predicted values, typically

ℋf={𝟏{f(X)=v};v∈𝒱}=𝟏{X∈f−1(v):v∈𝒱}.\mathcal{H}_{f}=\{{\mathbf{1}}\{f(X)=v\};v\in\mathcal{V}\}={\mathbf{1}}\{X\in f^{-1}(v):v\in\mathcal{V}\}.

This form (4) also appears in Gopalan et al. (2022) in achieving low-degree multicalibration. If f⁡(X)f(X) is continuous in practice, one replaces exact values by value intervals (buckets):

𝟏{f(X)∈Il}=𝟏{X∈f−1(Il)}=𝟏{X∈Sl},l=1,…,L.{\mathbf{1}}\{f(X)\in I_{l}\}={\mathbf{1}}\{X\in f^{-1}(I_{l})\}={\mathbf{1}}\{X\in S_{l}\},\quad l=1,\ldots,L.

This explains the bucketized boosting updates in Algorithm 2, where the auditor inspects conditional calibration across both feature groups and value ranges of ff.

The earlier MCBoost version (Kim et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2022) also offers an option that is based on the initial predictor f(0)f^{(0)}, corresponding to auditors of the form

h1(X)𝟏{f(0)(X)=v}=h1(X)𝟏{X∈f(0)−1(v)}.h_{1}(X){\mathbf{1}}\{f^{(0)}(X)=v\}=h_{1}(X){\mathbf{1}}\{X\in f^{(0)-1}(v)\}.

In quantile regression, as we shall see in the next subsection, ℋaud={∑G∈𝒢βG𝟏{X∈G}:G∈𝒢}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\beta_{G}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}:G\in\mathcal{G}\} in BatchGCP algorithm of Jung et al. (2022), or ℋaud={βG,v𝟏{X∈G}𝟏{qτ(X)=v}}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{\beta_{G,v}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}{\mathbf{1}}\{q_{\tau}(X)=v\}\} in BatchMVP (Jung et al., 2022). These examples illustrate the versatility of multicalibration, which covers the subgroup fariness and joint calibration over covariate-prediction slices.

2.3 Quantile regression as an example

For level τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1), the pinball loss can be written as

Lτ(Y,q)=(Y−q)(τ−𝟏{Y≤q}),∂qLτ(Y,q)={𝟏{Y≤q}−τ,𝟏{Y<q}−τ}L_{\tau}(Y,q)=(Y-q)(\tau-{\mathbf{1}}\{Y\leq q\}),\quad\partial_{q}L_{\tau}(Y,q)=\{{\mathbf{1}}\{Y\leq q\}-\tau,{\mathbf{1}}\{Y<q\}-\tau\} (5)

suph∈ℋ|𝔼[h(X,qτ(X))⋅s(Y,qτ(X))]|=suph∈ℋ|𝔼[h(X,qτ(X))⋅(𝟏{Y≤qτ(X)}−τ)]|<α,\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\big|\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(X,q_{\tau}(X))\cdot s(Y,q_{\tau}(X))\right]\big|=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\big|\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[h(X,q_{\tau}(X))\cdot(\mathbf{1}\{Y\leq q_{\tau}(X)\}-\tau)\right]\big|<\alpha, (6)

meaning the frequency of Y≤qτ​(X)Y\leq q_{\tau}(X) is τ\tau up to α\alpha-error for every slice hh. In other words, calibration at level τ\tau holds not just marginally but uniformly over the audited subpopulations included in ℋ\mathcal{H}.

With a single global bucket and choose

ℋaud={∑GβG𝟏{X∈G}∣G∈𝒢},\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\left\{\sum_{G}\beta_{G}\mathbf{1}\{X\in G\}\mid G\in\mathcal{G}\right\},

Example 2 (Multicalibration over (G,v)(G,v) bucket (MultiMVP))

Discretize [0,1][0,1] and let

ℋaud={βG,v𝟏{X∈G,qτ(X)=v}∣G∈𝒢,v∈[1/L]},\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{\beta_{G,v}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G,q_{\tau}(X)=v\}\mid G\in\mathcal{G},v\in[1/L]\},

This is equivalent to MultiMVP (Algorithm 2 in Jung et al. (2022); cf. Roth (2022)). Readers can find the details in Section D of Appendix.

2.4 From audit class to calibrated class

We are interested in characterizing the function class ℋ\mathcal{H} appearing in (1). It is essential to distinguish between audit class ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}, the collection explored by the auditor during training, and the multicalibrated class ℋ\mathcal{H}. Earlier work often assumed ℋ=ℋaud\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}, so eliminating empirical violations over ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} implied α\alpha-multicalibration (Deng et al., 2023). Other treatment sidestepped the issue by postulating an unspecified class ℋ\mathcal{H} that is “agnostically learned” (Kim et al., 2019) at finite samples #​V=Θ⁡(N)\#V=\Theta(N), i.e.,

suph∈ℋ|1N​∑i∈Vh⁡(Xi)​s​(Yi,f~​(Xi))|<α,\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in V}h(X_{i})s(Y_{i},\widetilde{f}(X_{i}))\right|<\alpha,

leading to suph∈ℋ|𝔼​h​(X)​s​(Y,f~​(X))|=O⁡(α)\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}|\mathbb{E}h(X)s(Y,\widetilde{f}(X))|=O(\alpha) via concentration. In our formulation, the additional normalization introduced in (3) unlike Kim et al. (2019); Kim et al. (2022), facilitates a shaper theoretical analysis. Their assumption is not entirely without basis, since stopping criterion implicitly selects a class ℋ\mathcal{H} for which the empirical multicalibration condition holds. At minimum, following the unnormalized stopping criterion, any hh belonging to the convex hull of final audit functions {hB,Sl}l=1L\{h_{B,S_{l}}\}_{l=1}^{L} automatically satisfies (1). Thus, one can at least conclude ℋ⊃Conv​({hB,Sl}l=1,…,L)\mathcal{H}\supset\textrm{Conv}(\{h_{B,S_{l}}\}_{l=1,\ldots,L}).

Remark 1

We observe that Deng et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024) implicitly assume access to a black-box optimization oracle together with exact knowledge of the underlying distribution, as also discussed by Gibbs et al. (2025). Their procedure requires verifying whether all h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} are multicalibrated, which may only be feasible when ℋ\mathcal{H} is finite (for example, indicators of a fixed collection of sensitive groups). For general infinite classes, such an exhaustive check is generally not computationally tractable. Moreover, the updates presuppose a direct evaluation of expectations 𝔼​h⋅s\mathbb{E}h\cdot s, which in practice would require knowing the distribution exactly. The algorithm looks more like sketches: the choice of parameters and sample sizes is not fully specified, and the auditing step is left abstract. If hh is unknown, it must be approximated through some auxiliary procedure 𝒜\mathcal{A}, while in the simplest case where hh step functions on sensitive groups, the update reduces to constant adjustment within each group.

We make this relationship explicit. Formally, define the sequences of additive expansions

ℱk={∑j=1kηj​hj:hj∈ℋaud},ℱ=⋃k≥1ℱk¯,\mathcal{F}_{k}=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{j}:h_{j}\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}\right\},\quad\mathcal{F}=\overline{\bigcup_{k\geq 1}\mathcal{F}_{k}},

where the closure is taken in L2​(ℙX)L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}). We prove (Theorem 2) that the limit predictor f(∞)f^{(\infty)} satisfies

⟨g(∞),h⟩=0,∀h∈ℱ,g(∞)=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f(∞))|X].\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle=0,\quad\forall h\in\mathcal{F},\qquad g^{(\infty)}=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f^{(\infty)})|X].

Despite that |⟨g(∞),h⟩|=0,∀h∈ℱ|\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle|=0,\forall h\in\mathcal{F}, a practical algorithm halts after finitely many iterations BB on finite data. The resulting predictor f~=f(B)\widetilde{f}=f^{(B)} is multicalibrated over some ℋ\mathcal{H} with tolerance α\alpha, but we cannot claim ℋ\mathcal{H} to be the entire ℱ\mathcal{F}; the distinction is subtle but important. While the ideal limit f(∞)f^{(\infty)} is uncorrelated with all directions in the closure of the boosting span ℱ\mathcal{F}, the finite-step predictor merely achieves small, but nonzero, correlation |𝔼​h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B))||\mathbb{E}h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)})|.

Observe that scaling hh trivially rescales the correlation:

|𝔼​a⋅h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B)​(X))|=|a|​|𝔼⁡[h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B)​(X))]|.\displaystyle|\mathbb{E}a\cdot h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)}(X))|=|a||\mathbb{E}[h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)}(X))]|.

Hence, without constraining the the magnitude of hh, the notion of “multicalibrated over ℱ\mathcal{F}” becomes ill-posed: arbitrary large L2L_{2}-norms would yield unbounded violations. It is therefore meaningful to assess multicalibration within norm-bounded subset of ℱ\mathcal{F}. Concretely, if the algorithm halts at step BB with empirical violation below α\alpha, then

|𝔼​h​s​(Y,f(B)​(X))|=O⁡(‖h‖L2​α),∀h∈ℱ,|\mathbb{E}hs(Y,f^{(B)}(X))|=O(\|h\|_{L_{2}}\alpha),\forall h\in\mathcal{F},

and consequently,

supf∈ℱ,‖h‖L2≤Cℱ|𝔼​h​s​(Y,f(B)​(X))|=O⁡(Cℱ​α).\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F},\|h\|_{L_{2}}\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}}|\mathbb{E}hs(Y,f^{(B)}(X))|=O(C_{\mathcal{F}}\alpha).

This establishes that f(B)f^{(B)} is multicalibrated over the norm-bounded subspace of ℱ\mathcal{F}, with violation scaling linearly in the L2L_{2}-radius CℱC_{\mathcal{F}}. Details and formal results appear in the following sections.

Example 3

Each audit direction hjh_{j} may depend on XX, on the current predictor f(j)f^{(j)}, or occasionally on the initial predictor. Typical examples include:

  1. 1.

    Groupwise refinements:

    ℱk={∑j=1kηjβGj,j𝟏{X∈Gj:Gj∈𝒢}}={∑G∈𝒢(∑j:Gj=GηjβGj,j)𝟏{X∈G}}.\mathcal{F}_{k}=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}\beta_{G_{j},j}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G_{j}:G_{j}\in\mathcal{G}\}\right\}=\left\{\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}}(\sum_{j:G_{j}=G}\eta_{j}\beta_{G_{j},j}){\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}\right\}.
  2. 2.

    Additive tree ensembles: ℱk={∑j=1kηj​h1,j​(X)}\mathcal{F}_{k}=\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{1,j}(X)\}, with tree-based h1,jh_{1,j}.

  3. 3.

    Hybrid refinements combining trees and groups:

    ℱk={∑j=1kηj​h1,j​(X)​𝟏​{X∈Gj:Gj∈𝒢}}.\mathcal{F}_{k}=\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{1,j}(X){\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G_{j}:G_{j}\in\mathcal{G}\}\}.
  4. 4.

    Fixed-bucket refinements based on f(0)f^{(0)}:

    ℱk={∑j=1kηj​h1,j​(X)​𝟏​{f(0)​(X)∈Ilj;lj=1,…,L}}.\mathcal{F}_{k}=\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{1,j}(X){\mathbf{1}}\{f^{(0)}(X)\in I_{l_{j}};l_{j}=1,\ldots,L\}\}.
  5. 5.

    Dynamic bucket refinements using current predictions:

    ℱk\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{k} ={∑j=1kηjh1,j(X)𝟏{f(j)(X)∈Il}}={∑j=1kηjh1,j(X)𝟏{f(0)+∑u<jηuhu)(X)∈Il}}.\displaystyle=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{1,j}(X){\mathbf{1}}\{f^{(j)}(X)\in I_{l}\}\right\}=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{1,j}(X){\mathbf{1}}\{f^{(0)}+\sum_{u<j}\eta_{u}h_{u})(X)\in I_{l}\}\right\}.

These constructions illustrate that the expressive capacity of MCBoost depends crucially on the auditing algorithms and classes ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} that serve for different purposes. For example, group indicators mitigate group-wise disparities, bucketization enforces value-level calibration (Roth, 2022).

The preceding discussion clarifies that the true multicalibrated space need not coincide with the original class. Formally, we have ℋaud⊆ℱ=∪k≥1ℱk¯\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}\subseteq\mathcal{F}=\overline{\cup_{k\geq 1}\mathcal{F}_{k}}. The set ℱ\mathcal{F} thus represents the closure of all directions reachable by iterative boosting. In special cases, such as space spanned by finite-dimensional bases or partition indicators, do we have equality ℱ=ℋaud¯=ℋaud\mathcal{F}=\overline{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}=\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}. In general, ℱ\mathcal{F} can be strictly larger: for instance, additive expansions of regression trees or weak classifiers yield rich, infinite-dimensional spaces. Boosting implicitly expands the calibration domain from ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} to ℱ\mathcal{F}, providing a rigorous characterization of the learned multicalibrated class and formalizing what earlier work treated heuristically.

3 Theory of MCBoost and its empirical implications

We now turn to the formal theoretical analysis of the multicalibration boosting procedure. Our goal is to articulate the statistical and algorithmic principles underlying MCBoost and to clarify several aspects that have remained partially understood in prior work. Specifically, we investigate: i) the limiting behavior of the boosting trajectory: to what function does the predictor sequence converge and at what rate? ii) for which function family the predictor achieves multicalibration; and iii) the practical validity of finite-step stopping—does the halting rule guarantee multicalibration, and how does the iteration number relate to sample size and stopping threshold? To address these questions, we introduce some conditions and notation.

Condition 1

For every realized predictor ff along the boosting path, the map X↦h⁡(X,f⁡(X))X\mapsto h(X,f(X)) is measurable and the corresponding auditing family satisfies

suph∈ℋaud‖h‖L2≤Cℋaud<∞,\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}\|h\|_{L_{2}}\leq C_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}<\infty,

so every admissible audit direction lies in L2​(ℙX)L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}).

This holds for all indicator-bucket and bounded tree-based auditors.

Notation.

Let

ℒ⁡(f):=𝔼⁡[L⁡(Y,f⁡(X))],\mathcal{L}(f)\ :=\ \mathbb{E}\big[L\big(Y,f(X)\big)\big],

denote the population risk. For any g,h∈L2​(ℙX)g,h\in L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}), write

⟨g,h⟩:=𝔼⁡[g⁡(X)​h​(X)],‖h‖L2:=⟨h,h⟩\langle g,h\rangle:=\mathbb{E}[g(X)h(X)],\quad\|h\|_{L_{2}}:=\sqrt{\langle h,h\rangle}

If ss involves both XX and YY, we also use the shorthand

⟨s,h⟩=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))​h​(X)].\langle s,h\rangle=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f(X))h(X)].

The conditional mean score at iteration bb is g(b)​(X):=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f(b)​(X))∣X]g^{(b)}(X):=\mathbb{E}\!\left[s\!\left(Y,f^{(b)}(X)\right)\mid X\right], so that ⟨s(b),h⟩=⟨g(b),h⟩,\langle s^{(b)},h\rangle=\langle g^{(b)},h\rangle, for all h⁡(X)h(X).

The boosting dynamics depend on an auditing class ℋaud⊂L2​(ℙX)\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}\subset L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}). Let

ℱk:={∑j=1kηj​hj:hj∈ℋaud},ℱ:=⋃k≥1ℱk¯,\mathcal{F}_{k}\ :=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\eta_{j}h_{j}:h_{j}\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}\right\},\qquad\mathcal{F}\ :=\ \overline{\bigcup_{k\geq 1}\mathcal{F}_{k}}, (7)

For instance, if ℋ\mathcal{H} is the class of fixed-depth regression trees, then ℱ\mathcal{F} is the closure of all finite additive expansions of such trees, a rich additive function space. We then define the restricted dual norm

∥g∥∗:=sup{⟨g,h⟩:h∈ℱ,∥h∥L2≤1}.\|g\|_{*}\ :=\ \sup\{\,\langle g,h\rangle:\ h\in\mathcal{F},\ \|h\|_{L_{2}}\leq 1\,\}.

3.1 The limit of boosting procedure

We begin with a smoothness condition on the loss.

Definition 2 (Lipschitz derivative)

We say LL is cLc_{L}-smooth in its first argument if its score is 2​cL2c_{L}-Lipschitz: |s⁡(Y,u)−s⁡(Y,u)|≤2​cL​|u−v||s(Y,u)-s(Y,u)|\leq 2c_{L}|u-v| a.s. in YY.

This condition yields a standard quadratic lower bound,

Lemma 1

Suppose LL has cLc_{L}-smooth, the objective function LL we consider satisfy

L⁡(Y,f⁡(X))−L⁡(Y,f~​(X))≥∂uL⁡(Y,u)|u=f​(f⁡(X)−f~​(X))−cL​(f⁡(X)−f~​(X))2,L(Y,f(X))-L(Y,\widetilde{f}(X))\geq\partial_{u}L(Y,u)|_{u=f}(f(X)-\widetilde{f}(X))-c_{L}(f(X)-\widetilde{f}(X))^{2},

for some cL>0c_{L}>0, where ∂uL⁡(Y,u)\partial_{u}L(Y,u) is partial derivative/subgradient w.r.t the second argument uu.

The cLc_{L}-smooth condition holds for L=(Y−f⁡(X))2/2L=(Y-f(X))^{2}/2 and the pinball loss. Next we impose a weak-learning condition.

Condition 2 (Weak learner edge)

At iteration bb, the selected wost-violated direction h(b)∈ℋaudh^{(b)}\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} satisfies

⟨g(b),h(b)⟩‖h(b)‖L2≥κ​suph∈ℱ⟨g(b),h⟩‖h‖L2=κ​‖g(b)‖∗,g(b)​(X):=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f(b)​(X))∣X],\frac{\langle g^{(b)},h^{(b)}\rangle}{\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}}\ \geq\ \kappa\,\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{\langle g^{(b)},h\rangle}{\|h\|_{L_{2}}}\ =\ \kappa\,\|g^{(b)}\|_{*},\quad g^{(b)}(X):=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f^{(b)}(X))\mid X],

for some κ∈(0,1]\kappa\in(0,1], where ‖g‖∗:=sup‖h‖2≤1,h∈ℱ⟨g,h⟩\|g\|_{*}:=\sup_{\|h\|_{2}\leq 1,\,h\in\mathcal{F}}\langle g,h\rangle.

This condition requires that the weak learner consistently identifies a direction that is non-trivially aligned with the gradient (or residual) g(b)g^{(b)}. In other words, although the optimal update would be the exact maximizer h∗=arg​max‖h‖L2=1,h∈ℱ⁡⟨g(b),h⟩,h^{*}=\argmax_{\|h\|_{L_{2}}=1,h\in\mathcal{F}}\langle g^{(b)},h\rangle, we only ask that the learner returns a hypothesis whose correlation with g(b)g^{(b)} is a fixed fraction κ\kappa of this optimum. This “edge” assumption guarantees sufficient progress for refinement and convergence, even if the maximizer cannot be computed exactly in practice. Similar weak-learning hypotheses can been seen in earlier work such as Zhang and Yu (2005). Alon et al. (2021) and Freund and Schapire (1997) assume that each weak learner performs slightly better than chance, and the cumulative effect of such small improvements yields a strong final predictor. Our condition plays the same role here: each audit step only needs to make nontrivial progress in the direction of the current score.

To accommodate general losses beyond the squared loss, we measure the discrepancy via the generalized Bregman divergence

Dℒ​(f1,f2,ζ)=ℒ⁡(f1)−ℒ⁡(f2)−⟨ζ,f1−f2⟩,ζ∈∂ℒ⁡(f2),D_{\mathcal{L}}(f_{1},f_{2};\zeta)=\mathcal{L}(f_{1})-\mathcal{L}(f_{2})-\langle\zeta,f_{1}-f_{2}\rangle,\quad\zeta\in\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{2}),

where ∂ℒ⁡(f2)\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{2}) is the subderivatives at f2f_{2}. Alongside, we define the associated (possibly set-valued) Bregman projection

𝒫f(0)+ℱℒ​(f1,ζ):=arg​minf∈f(0)+ℱ⁡Dℒ​(f,f1,ζ),\mathcal{P}_{f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}^{\mathcal{L}}(f_{1};\zeta):=\argmin_{f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}D_{\mathcal{L}}(f,f_{1};\zeta),

that project the function f1f_{1} onto f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}.

Remark 2

A typical Bregman divergence

Dℒ​(f1,f2)=ℒ⁡(f1)−ℒ⁡(f2)−⟨∇ℒ​(f2),f1−f2⟩,D_{\mathcal{L}}(f_{1},f_{2})=\mathcal{L}(f_{1})-\mathcal{L}(f_{2})-\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(f_{2}),f_{1}-f_{2}\rangle,

requires the distance generating function (ℒ\mathcal{L} in our context) to be smooth and strictly (or strongly convex), Under which D⁡(f1,f2)=0D(f_{1},f_{2})=0 implies f1≡f2f_{1}\equiv f_{2}. For non-smooth convex losses (e.g., pinball loss), we work with subgradients. To speak of projection, it often requires 𝒫f(0)+ℱℒ​(f1,ζ)\mathcal{P}_{f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}^{\mathcal{L}}(f_{1};\zeta) to be unique; we extend this notion to allow it to be a set that accommodates multiple projected functions. Check Section A in the Appendix for more details.

Theorem 2 (Stationary and projection)

Suppose LL is cLc_{L}-smooth and Conditions 1, 2 hold. Let the step size at iteration bb be η(b)=⟨h(b),s⁡(Y,f(b))⟩2​cL​‖h(b)‖L22\eta^{(b)}=\tfrac{\langle h^{(b)},s(Y,f^{(b)})\rangle}{2c_{L}\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}} such that {‖∑b=1kη(b)​h(b)‖L2}k≥1\{\|\sum_{b=1}^{k}\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}\}_{k\geq 1} forms a Cauchy sequence in L2​(ℙX)L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}). Then the boosting iterates {f(b)}b≥0\{f^{(b)}\}_{b\geq 0} lie in f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F} and satisfy

ℒ⁡(f(0))≥ℒ⁡(f(1))≥⋯↓ℒ⁡(f(∞)).\mathcal{L}(f^{(0)})\;\geq\;\mathcal{L}(f^{(1)})\;\geq\;\cdots\;\downarrow\;\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}).

The limit f(∞)f^{(\infty)} is stationary in the affine span f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}:

⟨g(∞),h⟩= 0for all ​h∈ℱ,g(∞)​(X):=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f(∞)​(X))∣X].\ \langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle\ =\ 0\quad\text{for all }h\in\mathcal{F},\qquad g^{(\infty)}(X):=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f^{(\infty)}(X))\mid X].\

If the global minimizer f∗∈arg⁡minf⁡ℒ⁡(f)f^{*}\in\arg\min_{f}\mathcal{L}(f) exists, then

f(∞)∈𝒫f(0)+ℱℒ​(f∗,0)=arg​minf∈f(0)+ℱ⁡Dℒ​(f,f∗,0),f^{(\infty)}\in\mathcal{P}_{f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}^{\mathcal{L}}(f^{*};0)=\argmin_{f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}D_{\mathcal{L}}(f,f^{*};0),

i.e., the Bregman projection of f∗f^{*} onto the affine span f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}. Moreover,

arg​minf∈f(0)+ℱ⁡Dℒ​(f,f∗,0)=arg​minf∈f(0)+ℱ⁡ℒ​(f)\argmin_{f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}D_{\mathcal{L}}(f,f^{*};0)=\argmin_{f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}}\mathcal{L}(f)

is invariant of the choice of f∗f^{*}.

Theorem 2 uncovers that f(∞)f^{(\infty)} can be viewed as projection onto the set f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}. The initial predictor f(0)f^{(0)} need not lie in ℱ\mathcal{F}; it may arise from a different training procedure (e.g., linear regression or neural network) before refinement through tree or group-based boosting, and it may be well-trained or just inadvertently chosen. Nonetheless, the resulting limit is with respect to ℱ\mathcal{F},

suph∈ℱ|𝔼​s​(Y,f(∞))​h​(X)|=suph∈ℱ|⟨g(∞),h⟩|=0.\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F}}|\mathbb{E}s(Y,f^{(\infty)})h(X)|=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F}}|\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle|=0.

Thus, the learned multicalibrated class for f(∞)f^{(\infty)} is exactly the closed convex symmetric ℱ\mathcal{F}.

It would be instructive to investigate the gain from boosting under various form of ℱ\mathcal{F} and examine how the structure of the auditing family ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} influences the expansion of ℱ\mathcal{F}.

  1. 1.

    Finite basis. If ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} is a finite-dimensional linear subspace, e.g., ℋaud=span⁡{ϕ1,…,ϕK}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\mathrm{span}\{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{K}\} or a fixed set of group indicators {∑GβG𝟏{X∈G}:G∈𝒢}\{\sum_{G}\beta_{G}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}:G\in\mathcal{G}\}, then ℱ=ℋaud¯=ℋaud\mathcal{F}=\overline{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}=\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}. To expand calibration beyond this, the audit class itself has to be enlarged.

  2. 2.

    Rich dictionary. If ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} is an infinite dictionary of simple atoms, such as all depth-dd trees with arbitrary thresholds or all decision stumps sgn⁡(X−t),t∈ℝ\mathrm{sgn}(X-t),\,t\in\mathbb{R} (Bickel et al., 2006), then ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} grows genuinely with kk. For example, kk decision stumps on ℝ\mathbb{R} yield piecewise-constant functions with up to k+1k+1 intervals; sums of TT depth-dd trees are constant on the common refinement of TT partitions, with at most (2d)T(2^{d})^{T} cells. In this regime ℱ\mathcal{F} is infinite-dimensional, and its growth with kk precisely captures the “weak-to-strong” expressivity gain attributed to boosting. As kk increases, the multicalibration guarantee over ℱ\mathcal{F} quantifies this expressive power rigorously.

3.2 Projection operator: existence and limit characterization

When an optional projection onto a closed convex set O⊂L2​(ℙX)O\subset L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}) is used each round (e.g., O:={f:𝒳→[0,1]}O:=\{f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]\} ), the update becomes

f(b+1)=𝒫O​(f(b)−η(b)​h(b)).f^{(b+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{O}(f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)}).

Since OO need not be symmetric or affine, we adopt a mild operational hypothesis to control the projection step.

Condition 3 (Working Hypothesis)

Let O∈L2​(ℙX)O\in L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}) be a closed convex set.

  • •

    Inactive projection. The projection becomes inactive beyond some finite iteration B′B^{\prime}, i.e.,

    f(b+1)=𝒫O​(f(b)−η(b)​h(b))=f(b)−η(b)​h(b), for all ​b>B′.f^{(b+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{O}(f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)})=f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)},\text{ for all }b>B^{\prime}.
  • •

    Interior-at-limit. The limit f(∞)∈Int​(O)f^{(\infty)}\in\text{Int}(O), where Int​(O)\text{Int}(O) is the interior of OO: there is a positive margin to the boundary. Meanwhile, f(∞)±t​h∈Of^{(\infty)}\pm th\in O for all h∈ℱh\in\mathcal{F} with sufficiently small tt.

This condition is weaker and more realistic than requiring ℒ⁡(𝒫O​(⋅)≤ℒ⁡(⋅)CLOSE.\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}_{O}(\cdot)\leq\mathcal{L}(\cdot). at every step (Deng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024), which generally fails for arbitrary convex ℒ\mathcal{L} and OO. It is safer and standard to propose Condition 3 to handle projection steps in convex optimization. Then, we can reach the conclusion similar to 2.

Theorem 3

Under Conditions 1-3, with cLc_{L}-smooth LL and step size in Theorem 2, the sequence ℒ⁡(f(b))\mathcal{L}(f^{(b)}) is eventually nonincreasing (for all b>B′b>B^{\prime}), and f(b)→f(∞)∈Int​(O)f^{(b)}\to f^{(\infty)}\in\text{Int}(O) in L2L_{2}. Moreover,

⟨g(∞),h⟩= 0for all ​h∈ℱ,g(∞)​(X):=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f(∞)​(X))∣X],\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle\ =\ 0\quad\text{for all }h\in\mathcal{F},\qquad g^{(\infty)}(X):=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f^{(\infty)}(X))\mid X],

and f(∞)f^{(\infty)} is a ℱ\mathcal{F}-stationary in the sense that ℒ⁡(f(∞))\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}) is optimal along directions in ℱ\mathcal{F}, i.e.,

ℒ⁡(f)≥ℒ⁡(f(∞)),∀f∈O,f−f(∞)∈ℱ.\mathcal{L}(f)\geq\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}),\quad\forall f\in O,\,f-f^{(\infty)}\in\mathcal{F}.

The Bregman projection identity generally does not hold because our search space is ℱ\mathcal{F} rather than the entire space. Therefore, f(∞)f^{(\infty)} may be differ from the global Bregman projection 𝒫Oℒ​(f∗,0)=arg​minf∈O⁡Dℒ​(f,f∗,0)\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}(f^{*};0)=\argmin_{f\in O}D_{\mathcal{L}}(f,f^{*};0); however, the two coincides when no projection is presented. Indeed, the limit satisfies a restricted variational inequality (Rockafellar and Wets, 1998)

⟨g(∞),f−f(∞)⟩≥0,∀f∈O​ with ​f−f(∞)∈ℱ.\langle g^{(\infty)},f-f^{(\infty)}\rangle\geq 0,\quad\forall f\in O\text{ with }f-f^{(\infty)}\in\mathcal{F}.

This can be expressed in a general subdifferential form as 0∈𝒫ℱ​(∂ℒ⁡(f(∞))),0\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{F}}\left(\partial\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\right), which ensures

ℒ⁡(f(∞))≤ℒ⁡(f~),∀f~∈O,f~−f(∞)∈ℱ.\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\leq\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{f}),\quad\forall\widetilde{f}\in O,\widetilde{f}-f^{(\infty)}\in\mathcal{F}.

This directional stationary is weaker than the first-order optimality 𝒫Oℒ​(f∗,0)\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}(f^{*};0), and f(∞)f^{(\infty)} have a higher objective value if ℱ\mathcal{F} is not rich enough. More detailed discussion can be found in Section B.3. In other words, the stagewise limit f(∞)f^{(\infty)} need only be directionally stationary along ℱ\mathcal{F}, in contrast to 𝒫Oℒ​f∗\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}f^{*} which satisfies

⟨−∂ℒ(𝒫Oℒf∗),f−𝒫Oℒf∗⟩≤0,∀f∈O,\langle-\partial\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}f^{*}),f-\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}f^{*}\rangle\leq 0,\quad\forall f\in O,

which is a stronger condition than that required by f(∞)f^{(\infty)}, reflecting the possible difference between these two – f(∞)f^{(\infty)} may have a higher objective value if ℱ\mathcal{F} is not rich enough.

3.3 Convergence rates

Having established convergence of the boosting sequence, we next quantify the rate at which the excess risk Δb=ℒ⁡(f(b))−ℒ⁡(f(∞))\Delta_{b}=\mathcal{L}(f^{(b)})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}) vanishes. To this end, we posit an mild boundedness condition on the boosting path:

Condition 4 (Finite radius)

There exists R<∞R<\infty such that ‖f(b)−f(∞)‖L2≤R\|f^{(b)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}\leq R for all b≥0b\geq 0.

This condition says that all iterates remain in a L2L_{2}-ball around the limit, which is slightly stronger than the Cauchy condition ‖∑j=mnη(j)​h(j)‖L2→0,m,n→∞\|\sum_{j=m}^{n}\eta^{(j)}h^{(j)}\|_{L_{2}}\to 0,m,n\to\infty; indeed, ‖f(b)−f(∞)‖L2≤‖∑j=bB′η(j)​h(j)‖+ϵ\|f^{(b)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}\leq\left\|\sum_{j=b}^{B^{\prime}}\eta^{(j)}h^{(j)}\right\|+\epsilon for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and sufficient large B′B^{\prime}.

Theorem 4

Suppose LL is cLc_{L}-smooth and use the step η(b)=⟨g(b),h(b)⟩2​cL​‖h(b)‖L22.\eta^{(b)}=\dfrac{\langle g^{(b)},h^{(b)}\rangle}{2c_{L}\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}}. Under Conditions 1–4, the excess risk satisfies

ΔB≤4​cL​R2κ2⋅1B.\ \Delta_{B}\ \leq\ \frac{4c_{L}R^{2}}{\kappa^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{B}.

Theorem 4 elucidates an O⁡(1/B)O(1/B) convergence rate for excess risk under cLc_{L}-smooth condition. Stronger curvature assumptions can further accelerate convergence, such as L2L_{2} loss. In particular, if the loss satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition (Karimi et al., 2016), which is weaker than the strong convexity, the excess risk decays geometrically. Notably, our analysis only requires the PL condition with respect to the restricted dual norm on f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}, which is weaker than the usual global PL condition and aligns naturally with the structure induced by the boosting updates. For more general convex losses for which the cLc_{L}-smooth condition fails, the faster O⁡(1/B)O(1/B) and linear rates need not hold. In that case, the usual subgradient argument gives an O(B−1/2)O(B^{-1/2}) guarantee for the averaged iterate; see Appendix E.1.

To show that the PL condition yields linear rate, we define the μ\mu-PL condition as follows.

Definition 3 (Polyak-Łojasiewicz on restricted dual norm)

We say ℒ\mathcal{L} satisfies a μ\mu-PL condition (w.r.t. ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{*}) on f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F} if

12​‖g‖∗2≥μ⁡(ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f(∞)))for all ​f∈f(0)+ℱ,g=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))∣X].\frac{1}{2}\|g\|_{*}^{2}\ \geq\ \mu\,\big(\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\big)\quad\text{for all }f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F},\ g=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f(X))\mid X].
Theorem 5

Under cLc_{L}-smoothness, Condition 2, and the μ\mu-PL condition 3, the same step as in Theorem 4 yields

Δb+1≤(1−μ​κ22​cL)​Δb⟹ΔB≤(1−μ​κ22​cL)B​Δ0.\ \Delta_{b+1}\ \leq\ \Big(1-\frac{\mu\kappa^{2}}{2c_{L}}\Big)\Delta_{b}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Delta_{B}\ \leq\ \Big(1-\frac{\mu\kappa^{2}}{2c_{L}}\Big)^{B}\Delta_{0}.

For ℒ=𝔼​(Y−f)2/2\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}(Y-f)^{2}/2, the PL conditon holds automatically. Indeed, ℒ\mathcal{L} is 11-strongly convex:

ℒ⁡(f1)≥ℒ⁡(f2)+⟨∇ℒ​(f2),f1−f2⟩+12​‖f1−f2‖L22.\mathcal{L}(f_{1})\geq\mathcal{L}(f_{2})+\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(f_{2}),f_{1}-f_{2}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\|f_{1}-f_{2}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}.

Rearranging the above yields ℒ⁡(f(∞))−ℒ⁡(f)≥⟨∇ℒ​(f),f(∞)−f⟩+12​‖f(∞)−f‖L22,\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})-\mathcal{L}(f)\geq\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(f),f^{(\infty)}-f\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\|f^{(\infty)}-f\|_{L_{2}}^{2}, implying

‖g‖∗​‖f−f∞‖≥⟨∇ℒ​(f),f−f(∞)⟩≥μ12​‖f(∞)−f‖L22,∀f∈f(0)+ℱ,\|g\|_{*}\|f-f^{\infty}\|\geq\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(f),f-f^{(\infty)}\rangle\geq\frac{\mu_{1}}{2}\|f^{(\infty)}-f\|_{L_{2}}^{2},\forall f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F},

where μ1=1\mu_{1}=1 for squared loss. This gives the Error Bound (EB) condition

‖g‖∗≥μ12​‖f(∞)−f‖L2.\|g\|_{*}\geq\frac{\mu_{1}}{2}\|f^{(\infty)}-f\|_{L_{2}}.

Combing EB and cLc_{L}-smoothness (cL=1/2c_{L}=1/2 here)

ℒ⁡(f)≤ℒ⁡(f(∞))+⟨∇ℒ​(f(∞)),f−f(∞)⟩+cL​‖f(∞)−f‖L22,∀f∈f(0)+ℱ,\mathcal{L}(f)\leq\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})+\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}),f-f^{(\infty)}\rangle+c_{L}\|f^{(\infty)}-f\|_{L_{2}}^{2},\forall f\in f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F},

yields

ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f(∞))≤cL​‖f(∞)−f‖L22≤cL​4μ12​‖g‖∗2,\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\leq c_{L}\|f^{(\infty)}-f\|_{L_{2}}^{2}\leq c_{L}\frac{4}{\mu_{1}^{2}}\|g\|_{*}^{2},

Thus,

12​‖g‖∗2≥μ128​cL​(ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f(∞))).\frac{1}{2}\|g\|_{*}^{2}\geq\frac{\mu_{1}^{2}}{8c_{L}}(\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})).

So the squared loss satisfies the μ\mu-PL condition with μ=1/4\mu=1/4.

Corollary 6

Under cLc_{L}-smoothness, Conditions 1-2, and the μ\mu-PL condition 3, ΔB=O⁡(α2)\Delta_{B}=O(\alpha^{2}) is guaranteed by

B≳1log⁡((1−μ​κ2/(2​cL))−1)​log⁡(Cℱ​2​Δ0α2),\displaystyle B\gtrsim\frac{1}{\log\!\big((1-\mu\kappa^{2}/(2c_{L}))^{-1}\big)}\,\log\!\Big(\frac{C_{\mathcal{F}}\sqrt{2\Delta_{0}}}{\alpha^{2}}\Big),

provided μ​κ/(2​cL)<1\mu\kappa/(2c_{L})<1.

Remark 3

The PL framework connects excess risk directly to calibration error. Indeed,

MCℱ​(f(B)):=suph∈ℱ,‖h‖L2≤Cℱ|𝔼​h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B)​(X))|≤Cℱ​‖g(B)‖∗,\mathrm{MC}_{\mathcal{F}}(f^{(B)}):=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F},\|h\|_{L_{2}}\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}}\left|\mathbb{E}h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)}(X))\right|\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}\|g^{(B)}\|_{*},

then ΔB\Delta_{B} is small if α>Cℱ​‖g(B)‖∗>Cℱ​2​μ​ΔB\alpha>C_{\mathcal{F}}\|g^{(B)}\|_{*}>C_{\mathcal{F}}\sqrt{2\mu\Delta_{B}}. For squared loss, more directly,

|𝔼​h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B)​(X))|=|𝔼​h⋅(f(∞)​(X)−f(B)​(X))|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)}(X))\right|=\left|\mathbb{E}h\cdot(f^{(\infty)}(X)-f^{(B)}(X))\right|
≤Cℱ​‖f(B)−f(∞)‖L2≤Cℱ​2μ1​ΔB=Cℱ​2​ΔB.\displaystyle\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}\|f^{(B)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu_{1}}\Delta_{B}}=C_{\mathcal{F}}\sqrt{2\Delta_{B}}.

Small excess risk ΔB\Delta_{B} immediately yields small multicalibration error. Compared with the O⁡(1/B)O(1/B) decay under smoothness alone, the μ\mu-PL condition provides a linear rate, showing that significantly fewer steps suffice to achieve a target excess risk, L2L_{2}-risk, and multicalibration level.

Remark 4

With a projection, the inactive projection condition (Condition 3) allows the algorithm to maintain the same convergence rates for sufficiently large BB (see Appendix C) and to retain the same multicalibrated class ℋ\mathcal{H}.

3.4 Finite-step guarantees for practical multicalibration

The preceding results established the asymptotic convergence of MCBoost. In practice, however, the algorithm operates with finite samples and halts after finitely many iterations according to the stopping criterion. This raises two natural questions: (I) Does the procedure necessarily terminate in finite time (given sufficient data)? (II) Does the stopping rule ensure that the resulting predictor is multicalibrated? We answer both affirmatively under the weak-learner edge condition.

3.4.1 Guaranteed finite termination.

In what follows, we regard both the calibration and validation sets as non-negligible fractions of the total sample N=N1+N2N=N_{1}+N_{2} in Algorithm 1, i.e., #​Ξ=Θ⁡(N),#​V=Θ⁡(N)\#\Xi=\Theta(N),\#V=\Theta(N), so that both the auditing and the violation evaluation steps are effective.

Condition 5

Along the boosting trajectory, the condition mean score ‖g(b)‖∞≤C~\|g^{(b)}\|_{\infty}\leq\widetilde{C}, and there exists an envelope function H⁡(⋅)H(\cdot) such that |h⁡(X)|≤H⁡(X)|h(X)|\leq H(X) with ‖H2‖L2<∞\|H^{2}\|_{L_{2}}<\infty. Both classes ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} and ℋaud2\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2} are VC classes with VC dimensions V⁡(ℋaud)=O⁡(V⁡(ℋaud2))V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})=O(V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2})). Moreover, a variance floor holds uniformly: ∑i=1N(h(b)​(Xi))2/N≥cℋaud2>0\sum_{i=1}^{N}(h^{(b)}(X_{i}))^{2}/N\geq c_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}^{2}>0.

Classes satisfying the VC condition include: (1) Two-layer neural networks

ℋaud={Acitvate​(w⊤​X+w0),w∈ℝd,w0∈ℝ}.\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{\text{Acitvate}(w^{\top}X+w_{0}),w\in\mathbb{R}^{d},w_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\}.

(2) Tree-basis functions ℋaud={𝟏{(−∞,a1]×⋯×(−∞,ad]:a1,…,ad∈ℝ}}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{{\mathbf{1}}\{(-\infty,a_{1}]\times\cdots\times(-\infty,a_{d}]:a_{1},\dots,a_{d}\in\mathbb{R}\}\}. (3) Finite-dimensional linear classes: ℋaud={w⊤ϕ(X):∥w∥2≤Cw,X∈ℝd}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{w^{\top}\phi(X):\|w\|_{2}\leq C_{w},X\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\} with ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, λmax​(Σ)<∞,Σ=𝔼​ϕ​(X)​ϕ⊤​(X)\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)<\infty,\Sigma=\mathbb{E}\phi(X)\phi^{\top}(X). Both the tree-based and neural-network classes have finite VC-dimensions, and their linear spans are dense in C⁡(U)C(U) for any compact subset U∈ℝdU\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (Zhang and Yu, 2005).

The above condition is weaker than the uniform boundedness condition ‖h‖∞≤Cℋaud,h∈ℋaud\|h\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}},h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} used in earlier work. For instance, one may have h=w⊤​X,‖w‖L2≤1h=w^{\top}X,\|w\|_{L_{2}}\leq 1 and H=‖X‖H=\|X\|, where XX itself need not be bounded. Classical concentration inequalities such as McDiarmid’s or Hoeffding’s apply in the bounded case; here, we rely on Dudley’s entropy integral with VC complexity to handle more general settings.

Proposition 7

Suppose Conditions 1, 5 hold and LL is cLc_{L}-smooth. Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the MCBoost algorithm stops in B=O⁡(ℒ⁡(f(0))−ℒ⁡(f(∞))α2)B=O\left(\frac{\mathcal{L}(f^{(0)})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})}{\alpha^{2}}\right) with the step size in Theorem 4 and N=Ω⁡(log⁡(B/δ)+V⁡(ℋaud)α2)N=\Omega\left(\frac{\log(B/\delta)+V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})}{\alpha^{2}}\right) samples. If, in addition, the loss satisfies μ\mu-PL condition, then the number of iteration reduces to B=O⁡(log⁡(ℒ⁡(f(0))−ℒ⁡(f(∞)𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸α2))B=O\left(\log(\tfrac{\mathcal{L}(f^{(0)})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}}{\alpha^{2}})\right) under the same sample complexity.

Earlier studies (Kim et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2024) considered settings with abundant data, drawing a new validation batch at each iteration; in that regime, the total sample requirement scales as N=Ω⁡(B⋅log⁡(1/δ)+V⁡(ℋaud)α2)N=\Omega\left(B\cdot\tfrac{\log(1/\delta)+V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})}{\alpha^{2}}\right) in Proposition 7. In contrast, when data are limited, one may take V=ΞV=\Xi, a common practice in boosting and conformal prediction. This result complements Theorem 4 and 5, the earlier results quantify the asymptotic rate of risk reduction, whereas Proposition 7 provides a finite-sample halting guarantee, linking the number of steps, the tolerance level α\alpha, and the sample size.

3.4.2 Validity of stopping rule.

Theorem 8

Under Conditions 1, 2 and 5, the algorithm stops at iteration BB with sample size NN, where BB and NN satisfy Proposition 7; then we have

|⟨g(B),h(B)⟩|‖h(B)‖L2<2​α\frac{|\langle g^{(B)},h^{(B)}\rangle|}{\|h^{(B)}\|_{L_{2}}}\ <2\alpha

Then ‖g(B)‖∗<2​α/κ\|g^{(B)}\|_{*}<2\alpha/\kappa and

|𝔼​h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B)​(X))|≤‖h‖L2​2​ακ.\left|\mathbb{E}h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)}(X))\right|\leq\|h\|_{L_{2}}\frac{2\alpha}{\kappa}.

Hence,

suph∈ℱ,‖h‖L2≤Cℱ|𝔼​h⋅s⁡(Y,f(B)​(X))|≤Cℱ​2​ακ.\sup_{h\in\mathcal{F},\|h\|_{L_{2}}\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}}\left|\mathbb{E}h\cdot s(Y,f^{(B)}(X))\right|\leq C_{\mathcal{F}}\frac{2\alpha}{\kappa}.

Theorem 8 shows that once the empirical violation statistic falls below the threshold α\alpha, the correlation between the score s⁡(Y,f(B))s(Y,f^{(B)}) based on f(B)f^{(B)} and any h∈ℱh\in\mathcal{F} is uniformly bounded by a constant proportional to its norm, the tolerance level α\alpha, and the weak-learner constant κ\kappa. The bound generally applies to any function hh representable within ℱ\mathcal{F}. In particular, when ℱ\mathcal{F} arises from an auditing family ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} consisting of indicator-type functions, such as group indicators, value-based partitions, or their finite combinations, their inherent boundedness ensures that the scaling factor remains controlled, so the multicalibration guarantee holds without concern for unbounded magnitudes of hh.

Taken together, Propositions 7 and Theorem 8 establish the practical soundness of the MCBoost procedure: it halts after finitely many steps under realistic sample sizes, and the stopping criterion itself certifies multicalibration of the learned predictor.

3.5 Empirical illustration: early stopping and overfitting

Theorem 2 relies on an ideal, adaptive (line-search-like) step size η(b)=⟨h(b),s⁡(Y,f(b))⟩2​cL​‖h(b)‖L22\eta^{(b)}=\tfrac{\langle h^{(b)},s(Y,f^{(b)})\rangle}{2c_{L}\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}} and assumes a Cauchy-boosting path, which is guaranteed when step sizes decay fast such that ∑b=1∞η(b)<∞\sum_{b=1}^{\infty}\eta^{(b)}<\infty (Appendix B.2), i.e., when the total step budget is bounded. Conversely, the Cauchy-increment condition on {η(b)​h(b)}\{\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)}\} along does not imply ∑b=1∞η(b)<∞\sum_{b=1}^{\infty}\eta^{(b)}<\infty. These assumptions differ from those in Zhang and Yu (2005), which require ∑b=1∞η(b)=∞\sum_{b=1}^{\infty}\eta^{(b)}=\infty and ∑b=1∞η(b)​2<∞\sum_{b=1}^{\infty}\eta^{(b)2}<\infty. Nevertheless, these considerations highlight the practical necessity of early-stopping as a regularization device. This is particularly relevant when cLc_{L} is unknown and one resorts to a small fixed step size for implementation. For least-squares boosting, Bühlmann and Yu (2003) shows that using a fix step with a powerful base learner can overtrack noise as b→∞b\to\infty, which eventually interpolates the data and causes overfitting.Zhang and Yu (2005) further formalizes early stopping through the cumulative step-size budget and emphasizes its role as a key regularization mechanism. Our experiments demonstrate that the same phenomenon carries over to MCBoost.

We revisit the simulation setup in Section 2.1. Throughout, MCBoost partitions the calibration data into |𝒢|×L|\mathcal{G}|\times L bins based on categorical group membership and prediction levels to promote groupwise calibration. We consider L∈{1,2,4}L\in\{1,2,4\} and either group by X(d)=(X6,X7)∈{0,1}2X^{(d)}=(X_{6},X_{7})\in\{0,1\}^{2} or not, which yields |𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1 (no grouping) or |𝒢|=4|\mathcal{G}|=4 (four demographic groups).

We evaluate the global excess convex risk [𝔼​(Y−f(b)​(X))2−𝔼​(Y−f∗​(X))2]/2\big[\mathbb{E}(Y-f^{(b)}(X))^{2}-\mathbb{E}(Y-f^{*}(X))^{2}\big]/2 as a function of the cumulative step size. Across a range of nominal step sizes, the optimal stopping point occurs in a nearly identical total step budget (Figure 2). Moreover, as the sample size increases, the optimal stopping point shifts later and the admissible stopping range widens. This pattern is consistent with the classical boosting view of early stopping as regularization (Zhang and Yu, 2005).

Notably, the same figure also reveal a trade-off in MCBoost between calibration and predictive accuracy. Incorporating more groups and finer bucket structures improves calibration (Section 4), but can slightly increase excess risk, particularly when the data are partitioned into many small cells. While traditional boosting directly optimizes global MSE, multicalibration imposes additional structural constraints. Consequently, the empirical ordering

Naive≥MCBoost≥Traditional boosting\textrm{Naive}\;\geq\;\textrm{MCBoost}\;\geq\;\textrm{Traditional boosting}

in optimal MSE (Figure 2) reflects the cost of enforcing calibration.

Figure 3 compares several stopping strategies: fixed total-step budgets of order NρN^{\rho} with ρ∈{1/4,1/6}\rho\in\{1/4,1/6\}, three-fold cross-validation, and patience-based rules (Detommaso et al., 2024). Cross-validation performs robustly across settings, while patience-based stopping tends to slightly underperform, as it allocates additional data for monitoring.

3.6 Target-independent learning under covariate shift

The multicalibration framework can be extended beyond the source distribution to ensure valid guarantees under covariate shift. Let 𝒟𝒮\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝒟𝒯\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}} denote the joint distributions of (X,Y)(X,Y) in the source and target domains, respectively, with density ratio

w⁡(X)=p⁡(X|D=𝒯)p⁡(X|D=𝒮)=ℙ⁡(D=𝒯|X)ℙ⁡(D=𝒮|X)​ℙ⁡(D=𝒮)ℙ⁡(D=𝒯).w(X)=\frac{p(X|D=\mathcal{T})}{p(X|D=\mathcal{S})}=\frac{\mathbb{P}(D=\mathcal{T}|X)}{\mathbb{P}(D=\mathcal{S}|X)}\frac{\mathbb{P}(D=\mathcal{S})}{\mathbb{P}(D=\mathcal{T})}.

Here DD denotes domain membership, 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒯\mathcal{T} represent the source and target domains, respectively. The key question is if a predictor f~\widetilde{f} that is multicalibrated on the source domain could implicitly indicate universal adaptability such that |𝔼𝒟𝒯s(Y,f~(X))]|\big|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}}}s(Y,\widetilde{f}(X))]\big| is small, and remain multicalibrated to some extent, i.e.,

|𝔼𝒟𝒯​[c⋅s⁡(Y,f~​(X))]|<α,∀c⁡(⋅)∈𝒞.\big|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}}}\big[c\cdot s(Y,\widetilde{f}(X))\big]\big|<\alpha,\quad\forall c(\cdot)\in\mathcal{C}.

for some function class.

Theorem 9 (Target-independent multicalibration under covariate shift)

Let (X,Y)∼𝒟𝒮(X,Y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}} denote the source distribution and (X,Y)∼𝒟𝒯(X,Y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}} the target distribution, with density ratio w⁡(X)w(X). Suppose the score function admits a decomposition:

s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))=s1​(Y,f⁡(X))+s2​(Y),s(Y,f(X))=s_{1}(Y,f(X))+s_{2}(Y),

and define the error of a propensity-score weighted estimator using weights w~\widetilde{w} as

Err⁡(τ(p​s)​(w~))=|𝔼𝒟𝒮​[(w~​(X)−w⁡(X))​s2​(Y)]|,\mathrm{Err}(\tau^{(ps)}(\widetilde{w}))=\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}}}[(\widetilde{w}(X)-w(X))s_{2}(Y)]\right|,

Assume further that f~\widetilde{f} is (ℋ,α)(\mathcal{H},\alpha)-multicalibrated on 𝒟𝒮\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{S}} and

‖𝔼⁡[s1​(Y,f⁡(X))|X]‖L2≤C~,‖𝔼⁡[s2​(Y)|X]‖L2≤C~.\|\mathbb{E}[s_{1}(Y,f(X))|X]\|_{L_{2}}\leq\widetilde{C},\quad\|\mathbb{E}[s_{2}(Y)|X]\|_{L_{2}}\leq\widetilde{C}.

Define

ℋ(Σ):={σ~𝒯(X)=ℙ(D=𝒯∣X)},\mathcal{H}(\Sigma):=\Big\{\widetilde{\sigma}_{\mathcal{T}}(X)=\mathbb{P}(D=\mathcal{T}\mid X)\Big\},

the class of shifts induced by the propensity scores. Then the following hold.

  1. (i)

    Universal adaptability. The target error satisfies

    Err𝒯​(f~):=|𝔼𝒟𝒯​s​(Y,f~)|≤C~​infh∈ℋ{‖w−h/C‖L2+‖h/C−w~‖L2}+Err⁡(τ(p​s)​(w~))+αC,\displaystyle\mathrm{Err}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widetilde{f}):=\Big|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}}}s(Y,\widetilde{f})\Big|\leq\ \widetilde{C}\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\{\|w-h/C\|_{L_{2}}+\|h/C-\widetilde{w}\|_{L_{2}}\}+\mathrm{Err}(\tau^{(ps)}(\widetilde{w}))+\tfrac{\alpha}{C},

    Err𝒯​(f~)≤Err⁡(τp​s​(w~))+C~​‖w−w~‖L2+α.\mathrm{Err}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widetilde{f})\leq\mathrm{Err}(\tau^{ps}(\widetilde{w}))+\widetilde{C}\,\|w-\widetilde{w}\|_{L_{2}}+\alpha.

    Furthermore, if w∗:=infw~∈ℋ⁡(Σ)‖w−w~‖L2w^{*}:=\inf_{\widetilde{w}\in\mathcal{H}(\Sigma)}\|w-\widetilde{w}\|_{L_{2}} and w∗=h∗/C∗w^{*}=h^{*}/C^{*} for some h∗∈ℋh^{*}\in\mathcal{H}, the predictor f~\widetilde{f} achieves Universal Adaptability:

    Err𝒯​(f~)≤Err⁡(τ(p​s)​(w∗))+C~​‖w−w∗‖L2+α/C∗.\displaystyle\mathrm{Err}_{\mathcal{T}}(\widetilde{f})\leq\mathrm{Err}(\tau^{(ps)}(w^{*}))+\widetilde{C}\ \|w-w^{*}\|_{L_{2}}+\alpha/C^{*}.

Theorem 9 establishes that multicalibration can be extended naturally to covariate shift settings. If the density ratio ww can be well-approximated within ℋ\mathcal{H}, the same boosting scheme yields predictors that adapt universally to new target distributions while preserving conditional calibration guarantees.

For concreteness, in regression with squared loss, s1​(Y,f⁡(X))=f⁡(X)s_{1}(Y,f(X))=f(X), s2=−Ys_{2}=-Y; in quantile regression (C~=1\widetilde{C}=1), s1(Y,qτ(X))=𝟏{Y≤qτ(X)},s2=−τs_{1}(Y,q_{\tau}(X))={\mathbf{1}}\{Y\leq q_{\tau}(X)\},s_{2}=-\tau, the target coverage error at level τ\tau obeys

|𝔼𝒟𝒯[(𝟏{Y≤q~τ(X)}−τ)]|<infh∈ℋ{∥w−h/C∥L2+∥h/C−w~)∥L2}+αC.\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{T}}}\left[\big({\mathbf{1}}\{Y\leq\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)\}-\tau\big)\right]\right|<\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\{\|w-h/C\|_{L_{2}}+\|h/C-\widetilde{w})\|_{L_{2}}\}+\tfrac{\alpha}{C}.

In particular, if ‖𝔼⁡[s1​(Y,f⁡(X))|X]‖∞,‖𝔼⁡[s2​(Y)|X]‖∞≤C~\|\mathbb{E}[s_{1}(Y,f(X))|X]\|_{\infty},\|\mathbb{E}[s_{2}(Y)|X]\|_{\infty}\leq\widetilde{C}, then the L2L_{2}-norms in the above bounds can be replaced by their L1L_{1} counterparts.

Empirical studies further corroborate these theoretical insights. Recent work (Kim et al., 2022; Ye and Li, 2025) demonstrates that multicalibrated predictors under covariate shift perform on par with, and often surpass, standard propensity-score reweighting estimators, both in overall and in subgroup-level performance. These results underscore the strength of multicalibration as a unified principle for achieving reliable generalization and fairness under distributional heterogeneity.

Remark 5
