The perspective underscores the universality of multicalibration: it extends to a family of target distribution once established on the source.

4 Numerical studies of auditor mechanisms and covariate shift

We now return to the simulation design introduced in Section 2.1 and use it to study the empirical mechanisms suggested by the theory. The focus is not on literal empirical verification of the exact rates or constants in the theory, but on understanding how auditor richness, group information, and shift structure shape the practical behavior of MCBoost.

4.1 Auditor expressivity, group information, and calibration error

We study how different auditing strategies, grouping structures, and prediction partitions modify the practical gains from MCBoost. Cross-validation is used for early stopping so that calibration gains are not driven by uncontrolled overfitting.

The first message is that the auditor’s expressivity is decisive. Figure 4, top picture, shows that without explicit group splitting (|𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1), constant auditors only deliver piecewise-constant bucket corrections. Such updates merely shift the predictor within each bucket and cannot capture residual structure in the feature space, so the gains in both calibration and MSE are small. By contrast, tree-based and linear auditors exploit covariate information to approximate conditional residuals, leading to much larger reductions in both bias and prediction error. This pattern is broadly consistent with the theory: more expressive auditors provide richer correction directions, although the practical gains still depend on how well those directions align with the residual structure. In particular, linear refinement, while still finite-dimensional, can be substantially more effective than constant correction.

Figure 4, middle picture, shows that introducing group partition (|𝒢|=4|\mathcal{G}|=4) makes even simple constant auditors more effective because group–bucket interactions directly target subgroup offsets. The resulting gains in calibration are noticeable, but MSE improvements remain limited (middle picture of Figure 5) because constant adjustments can only perform coarse mean shifts. More flexible auditors, such as trees, continue to provide great improvements by capturing heterogeneous structures beyond group-level offsets. These findings are further supported by the excess-risk trajectories in Appendix Figures 9, 10, 11, and 12. When |𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1, constant auditors tend to increase the global excess risk after only a few iterations for both linear and random forest initial learners, whereas tree-based auditors or explicit group partitioning (|𝒢|=4|\mathcal{G}|=4) generally lead to stable or decreasing excess risk.

Increasing the number of prediction buckets LL alone has a relatively small effect on groupwise performance. The mean bias and MSE curves are nearly unchanged across bucket choices, which suggests that finer prediction partitions are not by themselves the main source of improvement. The dominant factors are the expressive power of the auditor and whether the relevant group information is made available to it.

Another phenomenon concerns access to group information during audit. When there is no explicit group split (|𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1) and categorical variables are excluded from the residual fit (Figure 8), all methods show negligible improvement in mean calibration bias and only limited MSE gains. Auditors simply cannot distinguish latent subpopulations; without group-related features, the correction term is effectively homogeneous and cannot repair systematic group-specific discrepancies. Even flexible tree auditors fail in this regime because their partitions are built only from the observed covariates. In terms of MSE, the linear model shows worst error for all settings. Tree-based auditors likely reduce MSE the most, and constant correction does not improve MSE under |𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1.

By contrast, when samples are explicitly partitioned by group (|𝒢|=4|\mathcal{G}|=4) and X(d)X^{(d)} are included in the audit step (middle pictures of Figures 4 and 5), most methods reduce both MSE and bias. The main exception is constant refinement applied to an already well-specified linear model: if the initial predictor already satisfies the relevant linear moment conditions with the group features included, there is little left for a constant correction to do. However, when X(d)X^{(d)} is omitted from the initial fit, the same groupwise constant corrections become effective, which highlights the practical importance of injecting group structure either into the initial predictor or into the audit stage.

If group partitions are imposed but X(d)X^{(d)} is still excluded during residual fitting (Figure 4(c)), performance deteriorates again, especially for the calibration bias of the linear initial predictor. In that case, the correction can only enforce calibration along the observed feature space, for example through relations such as 𝔼⁡[X(c)⊤​(Y−f^)]=0\mathbb{E}[X^{(c)\top}(Y-\widehat{f})]=0, and cannot fully resolve hidden group-level misspecification.

Beyond the group level, we also examine calibration at a finer resolution by considering group–prediction-level pairs. We apply MCBoost to an initial random forest predictor in Figure 6, using a decision tree regressor as the auditor for iterative refinement. For each (G,l)(G,l), we evaluate the conditional calibration error 𝔼[Y−f(X)|f(X)∈Il,X∈G],\mathbb{E}[Y-f(X)|f(X)\in I_{l},X\in G], estimated empirically within each bin, where the prediction bins IlI_{l} partition the range of f⁡(X)f(X) into LL equal-length intervals. Because bucket boundaries depend on the fitted predictor and therefore vary across replications, the calibration errors are aggregated over repeated runs. In both settings (|𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1 and |𝒢|=4|\mathcal{G}|=4), MCBoost substantially reduces these conditional calibration errors, confirming that the method effectively corrects the systematic bias within the slices defined jointly by the group membership and the prediction level.

We also evaluate MCBoost for quantile regression under pinball loss, again with cross-validation used to determine the effective step-size budget. The qualitative picture is similar to the mean-regression case; Appendix Figures 13 and 14 plot the excess pinball los against the cumulative step size. In particular, improvements are more pronounced in underrepresented subpopulations (Figure 15), and the coverage of multicalibrated predictors is more tightly concentrated near the nominal level 0.90.9 (Figure 16). This suggests that the calibration mechanism extends beyond the squared loss and remains effective for distributional targets such as conditional quantiles.

4.2 MCBoost under distribution shift

We further investigate MCBoost under covariate shift. This experiment complements Theorem 9: the theory predicts gains when the target shift is well approximated by the learned multicalibration class. The demographic groups considered above can already be interpreted as special cases of covariate shift through localized weight functions of the form w(X)=𝟏{X∈G}/ℙ(G).w(X)={\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}/\mathbb{P}(G). Our goal here is to move beyond prespecified demographic groups and examine whether MCBoost remains effective on nonlinear structured subgroups and weighted shifts that are not explicitly hard-coded in advance. We evaluate mean bias and MSE in a collection of nonlinear structural subgroups and weighted shifts constructed from standardized covariates Z=(Z1,Z2)Z=(Z_{1},Z_{2}), corresponding to (X1(c),X2(c))(X^{(c)}_{1},X^{(c)}_{2}); full constructions are given in the Supplementary Section F.3.

These targets are intentionally more structured than the demographic groups used earlier. They are not aligned with simple linear partitions and therefore provide a sharper test of the effectiveness of the chosen auditor. Figure 7 shows that the benefits of MCBoost persist on these structured targets but depend on auditor’s expressivity. Constant and linear auditors show limited improvement in mean bias and MSE, yet tree-based auditors improve both metrics much more substantially. This is broadly consistent with the theoretical picture: more expressive auditors induce a richer cumulative boosting span, enabling better approximation of nonlinear subgroup structure and density shifts.

The practical implication is similar to the work on conditional guarantee and helps to answer the question of how to choose the auditor in practice. When target groups or probable forms of shift are known in advance, the audit class ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} should reflect that structure as closely as possible. However, when little is known a priori, more expressive auditors, such as trees, may provide a safer default because they are better able to adapt to nonlinear and interaction-driven discrepancies.

5 Discussion

This work provides a thorough investigation of the mechanisms through which MCBoost achieves multicalibration. Viewed as an extension of classical boosting, MCBoost inherits many familiar principles: the weak learner determines the approximation power, while early stopping helps control overfitting. Our theory clarifies the functional class that can ultimately be calibrated, establishes convergence rates under different smoothness conditions, and gives a finite-sample guarantee together with a valid termination rule, under relatively mild assumptions.

Our numerical results illustrate the motivation for multicalibration and the trade-off between optimal global predictive accuracy and improved calibration. We further evaluate the performance of MCBoost across different auditors, group partitions, and feature sets, considering hard-coded demographic groups, nonlinear data-driven subpopulations, and structured weighted shifts. Taken together, these results provide a clearer understanding of the MCBoost framework. We hope that this article can serve as a useful guide for practitioners seeking predictive models that are both reliable and transferable in practice.

More broadly, Algorithm 1 is not limited to the |𝒢|×L|\mathcal{G}|\times L partitions studied here. The auditing step can be based on richer, data-adaptive partitions of the covariate-prediction space, potentially targeting fairness across more complex regions. We leave an investigation of such extensions to future work. Our framework currently treats univariate predictors f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}. Extending the analysis to multivariate prediction problems with f⁡(X)∈ℝdf(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, or to scores that depend on additional objects such as the initial predictor f(0)f^{(0)} or a threshold function λ⁡(X)\lambda(X) (Zhang et al., 2024), is a natural next step. These extensions are conceptually straightforward and can be handled with minor modifications.

Appendix A Extended Bregman divergence with subgradient

The standard distance generating function (expected loss function ℒ\mathcal{L} in our article), which induces the Bregman divergence, needs to be differentiable and strictly (or strongly) convex functions, such as the squared loss. However, many objectives of interest, such as the pinball loss, are merely convex, not strictly convex, and are non-differentiable globally. To extend our analysis, we introduce a generalized Bregman divergence based on subgradients.

Recall that the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the expectation over L2​(ℙX)L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{X}), sometimes equivalently viewed as the expectation under the joint distribution of (Y,X)(Y,X).

The pinball loss Lτ​(Y,qτ​(X))L_{\tau}(Y,q_{\tau}(X)) admits a Lipschitz subgradient, so by Lemma 1 it satisfies

Lτ​(Y,qτ​(X))−Lτ​(Y,q~τ​(X))≥ζ⁡(Y,X)​(qτ​(X)−q~τ​(X)),L_{\tau}(Y,q_{\tau}(X))-L_{\tau}(Y,\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X))\geq\zeta(Y,X)(q_{\tau}(X)-\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)), (8)

where

ζ⁡(Y,X)={1−τ,Y<q~τ​(X),[−τ,1−τ],Y=q~​(X),−τ,Y>q~​(X).\zeta(Y,X)=\begin{cases}1-\tau,&Y<\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X),\\ [-\tau,1-\tau],&Y=\widetilde{q}(X),\\ -\tau,&Y>\widetilde{q}(X).\end{cases}

In other words,

ℒ⁡(qτ)−ℒ⁡(q~τ)≥⟨ζ⁡(Y,X,q~τ),qτ​(X)−q~τ​(X)⟩.\mathcal{L}(q_{\tau})-\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{q}_{\tau})\geq\langle\zeta(Y,X;\widetilde{q}_{\tau}),q_{\tau}(X)-\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)\rangle.

Since ζ\zeta depends on both XX and YY, we formally define the subderivatives of ℒ\mathcal{L} as

∂ℒ⁡(f):={ζ⁡(f):𝒳→ℝ},\partial\mathcal{L}(f):=\{\zeta(f):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\},

such that for any pairs of functions f,f~f,\widetilde{f},

ℒ⁡(f)−ℒ⁡(f~)≥⟨ζ⁡(f~),f−f~⟩,ζ⁡(f~)∈∂ℒ⁡(f~).\mathcal{L}(f)-\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{f})\geq\langle\zeta(\widetilde{f}),f-\widetilde{f}\rangle,\quad\zeta(\widetilde{f})\in\partial\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{f}).

For the pinball loss, the conditional subgradient is explicitly

ζ⁡(q~τ)∈{(1−τ)​ℙ​(Y<q~τ​(X)|X)−τ​ℙ​(Y>q~τ​(X)|X)+[−τ,1−τ]⋅ℙ⁡(Y=q~τ​(X)|X)}.\zeta(\widetilde{q}_{\tau})\in\left\{(1-\tau)\mathbb{P}(Y<\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)|X)-\tau\mathbb{P}(Y>\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)|X)+[-\tau,1-\tau]\cdot\mathbb{P}(Y=\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)|X)\right\}.

When Y|XY|X is continuous almost surely, the last term vanishes and ∂ℒ⁡(f)\partial\mathcal{L}(f) reduces to a singleton, recovering the usual differentiable case.

If ℒ\mathcal{L} is smooth, then ∂ℒ⁡(f)={∇ℒ​(f)}\partial\mathcal{L}(f)=\{\nabla\mathcal{L}(f)\}, where ∇ℒ​(f)\nabla\mathcal{L}(f) corresponds to the Gateaux derivative (Zhang et al., 2024) satisfying

⟨∇ℒ​(f),h⟩=∂∂ϵ​ℒ​(f+ϵ​h)|ϵ=0,∀h.\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(f),h\rangle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon}\mathcal{L}(f+\epsilon h)|_{\epsilon=0},\quad\forall h.

For quantile regression, sτ(Y,qτ)=𝟏{Y≤qτ}−τs_{\tau}(Y,q_{\tau})={\mathbf{1}}\{Y\leq q_{\tau}\}-\tau is indeed one of the subderivatives we choose for LτL_{\tau}, it could also be 𝟏{Y<qτ}−τ{\mathbf{1}}\{Y<q_{\tau}\}-\tau. These two do not make distinction when Y|XY|X is continuous and ∂ℒ\partial\mathcal{L} reduces to a singleton.

Generalized Bregman divergence.

Regarding all these, we define the generalized Bregman divergence as

Dℒ​(f1,f2,ζ)=ℒ⁡(f1)−ℒ⁡(f2)−⟨ζ⁡(f2),f1−f2⟩,ζ⁡(f2)∈∂ℒ⁡(f2).D_{\mathcal{L}}(f_{1},f_{2};\zeta)=\mathcal{L}(f_{1})-\mathcal{L}(f_{2})-\langle\zeta(f_{2}),f_{1}-f_{2}\rangle,\quad\zeta(f_{2})\in\partial\mathcal{L}(f_{2}).

The divergence depends on the specific choice of subgradient ζ\zeta.

Algorithmically, given Algorithmically, given the form of sτ​(Y,qτ)s_{\tau}(Y,q_{\tau}) in Subsection 2.3, we actually fit the “residual” sτ​(Y,qτ(b))s_{\tau}(Y,q_{\tau}^{(b)}) to approximate the subgradient

g(b)\displaystyle g^{(b)} :=𝔼⁡[sτ​(Y,qτ(b)​(X))|X]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}[s_{\tau}(Y,q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X))|X]
=(1−τ)​ℙ​(Y≤q~τ​(X)|X)−τ​ℙ​(Y>q~τ​(X)|X)\displaystyle=(1-\tau)\mathbb{P}(Y\leq\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)|X)-\tau\mathbb{P}(Y>\widetilde{q}_{\tau}(X)|X)
=:ζ⁡(qτ(b))​(X)\displaystyle=:\zeta(q_{\tau}^{(b)})(X)

at iteration bb. In the boosting procedure, we usually fix a consistent subgradient form during updates and do not very the subgradient form across iterations. When Y|XY|X is continuous a.s., both the population minimizer qτ∗​(X)q_{\tau}^{*}(X) and the boosting limit qτ​(X)q_{\tau}(X) are unique; otherwise, multiple minimizers (e.g., any median between two discrete points) may exist.

The generalized Bregman divergence retains key properties of its classical counterpart:

  • •

    Non-negativity. Dℒ​(f1,f2,ζ⁡(f2))≥0D_{\mathcal{L}}(f_{1},f_{2};\zeta(f_{2}))\geq 0 for any ζ∈∂ℒ\zeta\in\partial\mathcal{L}, a direct consequence of convexity and definition of subgradient.

When C=f(0)+ℱC=f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}, we have ⟨g(∞),h⟩=0,∀h∈ℱ\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle=0,\forall h\in\mathcal{F}. Having this is no stronger than the general optimality condition. The uniqueness is by strictly convexity, no-atom at the τ\tau-th quantile for pinball loss, or the use of regularizing like minimizing ℒ⁡(f)+λ​‖f‖L22,λ>0\mathcal{L}(f)+\lambda\|f\|_{L_{2}}^{2},\lambda>0. Consequently, it will select the one with minimal norm as λ→0\lambda\to 0.

B.3 Proof of Theorem 3

We now discuss the scenario in which the optional projection 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O} exists. For instance, OO represents the space of bounded functions taking values in [0,1][0,1]:

O:={f:𝒳→[0,1]},O:=\{f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]\},

which is closed and convex but not symmetric. With respect to the L2L_{2} norm, the projection takes the explicit form 𝒫O​f:X↦max⁡{min⁡{f⁡(X),1},0}\mathcal{P}_{O}f:X\mapsto\max\{\min\{f(X),1\},0\}.

Proof [Proof of Theorem 3] Under Condition 3 and the weak learner condition 2, the sequence {f(b)}\{f^{(b)}\} remains in OO, and {ℒ⁡(f(b))}\{\mathcal{L}(f^{(b)})\} forms monotonically nonincreasing for b>B′b>B^{\prime}, forsufficiently large B′B^{\prime}, since 𝒫O​(f(b)−η(b)​h(b))=f(b)−η(b)​h(b)\mathcal{P}_{O}(f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)})=f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)} by the inactive projection condition; and updating with small steps stay within OO. Consequently, by the same argument as before, we obtain

⟨g(∞),h⟩=0,∀h∈ℱ.\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle=0,\quad\forall h\in\mathcal{F}.
Restricted optimality.

A subtle but important observation is that no feasible ℱ\mathcal{F}-direction can reduce the loss since. Indeed,

ℒ⁡(f(∞))−ℒ⁡(f)≤⟨g(∞),f−f(∞)⟩≤0,∀f=f(∞)+t​h∈O,h∈ℱ.\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})-\mathcal{L}(f)\leq\langle g^{(\infty)},f-f^{(\infty)}\rangle\leq 0,\quad\forall f=f^{(\infty)}+th\in O,h\in\mathcal{F}.

If ‖g(∞)‖∗≠0\|g^{(\infty)}\|_{*}\neq 0, there would be some hh and t>0t>0 such that ℒ⁡(f(∞)+t​h)≤ℒ⁡(f(∞))\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}+th)\leq\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}), contradicting stationary.

Note, however, that f(∞)f^{(\infty)}, though lies in OO, may differ from

𝒫Oℒ​(f∗):=arg​minf∈O⁡Dℒ​(f,f∗,0),\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}(f^{*}):=\argmin_{f\in O}D_{\mathcal{L}}(f,f^{*};0),

because our search space of our algorithm is f(0)+ℱf^{(0)}+\mathcal{F} rather than the entire space. Suppose p∈𝒫Oℒ​(f∗)p\in\mathcal{P}_{O}^{\mathcal{L}}(f^{*}), then by convex optimality,

⟨−ζ⁡(p),f−p⟩≤0,∃ζ⁡(p)∈∂ℒ⁡(p),∀f∈O,\langle-\zeta(p),f-p\rangle\leq 0,\quad\exists\zeta(p)\in\partial\mathcal{L}(p),\forall f\in O,

which represents a different variational inequality from that satisfied by f(∞)f^{(\infty)}. The two coincide when no projection is present: O=f(0)+ℱO=f^{(0)}+\mathcal{F}.

Restricted variational inequality.

The limit f(∞)f^{(\infty)} satisfies a restricted variational inequality:

⟨g(∞),f−f(∞)⟩≥0,∀f∈O​ with ​f−f(∞)∈ℱ,\langle g^{(\infty)},f-f^{(\infty)}\rangle\geq 0,\forall f\in O\text{ with }f-f^{(\infty)}\in\mathcal{F}, (13)

where g(∞)=𝔼⁡[s⁡(Y,f⁡(X))|X]g^{(\infty)}=\mathbb{E}[s(Y,f(X))|X].

More generally, (13) can be expressed in subdifferential form as

0∈𝒫ℱ​(∂ℒ⁡(f(∞))),0\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{F}}\left(\partial\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\right),

which ensures

ℒ⁡(f)≤ℒ⁡(f~),∀f~∈O,f~−f∈ℱ.\mathcal{L}(f)\leq\mathcal{L}(\widetilde{f}),\quad\forall\widetilde{f}\in O,\widetilde{f}-f\in\mathcal{F}.

Our predictor guarantees ⟨g(∞),h⟩=0\langle g^{(\infty)},h\rangle=0 for specific g(∞)g^{(\infty)}. In words, the stagewise limit f(∞)f^{(\infty)} need only be directionally stationary along ℱ\mathcal{F}, in contrast to 𝒫O​f∗\mathcal{P}_{O}f^{*} which satisfies ⟨−∂ℒ(𝒫Of∗),f−𝒫Of∗⟩≤0\langle-\partial\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}_{O}f^{*}),f-\mathcal{P}_{O}f^{*}\rangle\leq 0. This condition is stronger than the variational inequality (VI) required by f(∞)f^{(\infty)}, reflecting the possible difference between these two – f(∞)f^{(\infty)} may have a higher objective value if ℱ\mathcal{F} is not rich enough.  

Example 4

A concrete example to separate the two estimator would be: ℒ⁡(f)=12​‖f−f∗‖22\mathcal{L}(f)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|f-f^{*}\|_{2}^{2} with f∗=(1,0)f^{*}=(1,0), ℱ=span​{e2}\mathcal{F}=\text{span}\{e_{2}\}, and O=[−10,10]2O=[-10,10]^{2}. The minimizer is 𝒫O​f∗=(1,0)\mathcal{P}_{O}f^{*}=(1,0). For the restricted problem: g(∞)=f(∞)−f∗g^{(\infty)}=f^{(\infty)}-f^{*}; projecting onto ℱ\mathcal{F} yields (f(∞))2=0(f^{(\infty)})_{2}=0. This shows any (f1,0)∈O(f_{1},0)\in O is ℱ\mathcal{F}-stationary, whereas only f1=1f_{1}=1 matches the global minimum.

Remark 6

MCBoost with optional projection can be interpretedas a proximal gradient descent (mirror descent) method with the L2L_{2}-distance:

f(b+1)=𝒫O​(f(b)−η(b)​h(b))=arg​minf∈O⁡{⟨η(b)​h(b),f⟩+12​‖f−f(b)‖L22}.f^{(b+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{O}(f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)})=\argmin_{f\in O}\left\{\langle\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)},f\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\|f-f^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}\right\}.

The three-point inequality ensures that

⟨−η(b)​h(b),f−f(b+1)⟩≤−DL2​(f,f(b+1))+DL2​(f,f(b))−DL2​(f(b+1),f(b))\langle-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)},f-f^{(b+1)}\rangle\leq-D_{L_{2}}(f,f^{(b+1)})+D_{L_{2}}(f,f^{(b)})-D_{L_{2}}(f^{(b+1)},f^{(b)})

Unlike standard projected gradient descent, boosting uses h(b)∈ℋaudh^{(b)}\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} as an approximation of the true gradient or subgradient g(b)g^{(b)}. Consequently,

ℒ⁡(f(b+1))−ℒ⁡(f(b))\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(f^{(b+1)})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(b)}) ≤⟨g(b),f(b+1)−f(b)⟩+cL​‖f(b+1)−f(b)‖L22\displaystyle\leq\langle g^{(b)},f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\rangle+c_{L}\|f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}
≤⟨h(b),f(b+1)−f(b)⟩+⟨g(b)−h(b),f(b+1)−f(b)⟩+cL​‖f(b+1)−f(b)‖L22\displaystyle\leq\langle h^{(b)},f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\rangle+\langle g^{(b)}-h^{(b)},f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\rangle+c_{L}\|f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}
≤(cL−1η(b))​‖f(b+1)−f(b)‖L22+⟨g(b)−h(b),f(b+1)−f(b)⟩.\displaystyle\leq\left(c_{L}-\frac{1}{\eta^{(b)}}\right)\|f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}+\langle g^{(b)}-h^{(b)},f^{(b+1)}-f^{(b)}\rangle.

We can obtain the same results presented in the proof of the main theorem if there is no 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O} – each iteration ensures sufficient descent.

Consequences for VC-type classes.

A lemma from Wellner and others (2013) connects the entropy with VC dimensions:

Lemma 14 (Theorem 2.6.7 of Wellner and others (2013))

For a VC-class of functions ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} with finite VC dimension V⁡(ℋaud)V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}), envelope function HH and p≥1p\geq 1, one has for any probability measure QQ with ‖H‖Lp​(Q)>0\|H\|_{L_{p}(Q)}>0,

𝒩⁡(ϵ​‖H‖Lp​(Q),ℋaud,Lp​(Q))≤C​(1ϵ)p⋅V⁡(ℋaud),0<ϵ<1.\mathcal{N}(\epsilon\|H\|_{L_{p}(Q)},\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}},L_{p}(Q))\leq C\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)^{p\cdot V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})},\quad 0<\epsilon<1.

Consequently, if both ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} and ℋaud2\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2} are VC classes with finite VC dimensions V⁡(ℋaud)V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}) and V⁡(ℋaud2)V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2}), then

J2​(ℋaud,Q)≲V⁡(ℋaud),J2​(ℋaud,Q)≲V⁡(ℋaud2),J_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}};Q)\lesssim\sqrt{V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})},\quad J_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}};Q)\lesssim\sqrt{V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2})},

and Lemma 13 yields the simplified rates

suph∈ℋaud|(PN−P)​h​(X)​g(b)​(X)|≲V⁡(ℋaud)+log⁡(1/δ)N,\displaystyle\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}|(P_{N}-P)h(X)g^{(b)}(X)|\lesssim\frac{\sqrt{V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})}+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{N}},
suph∈ℋaud|(PN−P)​h2|≲V⁡(ℋaud2)+log⁡(1/δ)N.\displaystyle\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}|(P_{N}-P)h^{2}|\lesssim\frac{\sqrt{V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2})}+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{N}}.

Some examples of classes satisfying the condition include: (1) Two-layer neural networks ℋaud={Acitvate​(w⊤​X+w0),w∈ℝd,w0∈ℝ}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{\text{Acitvate}(w^{\top}X+w_{0}),w\in\mathbb{R}^{d},w_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\}. (2) Tree-basis functions ℋaud={𝟏{(−∞,a1]×⋯×(−∞,ad]:a1,…,ad∈ℝ}}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{{\mathbf{1}}\{(-\infty,a_{1}]\times\cdots\times(-\infty,a_{d}]:a_{1},\dots,a_{d}\in\mathbb{R}\}\}. The tree-basis and neural network classes all have finite VC-dimensions, and span​(ℋaud)\text{span}(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}) is dense in C⁡(U)C(U) for any compact subset U∈ℝdU\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (Zhang and Yu, 2005). (3) Finite-dimensional linear classes: ℋaud={w⊤ϕ(X):∥w∥2≤Cw,X∈ℝd}\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{w^{\top}\phi(X):\|w\|_{2}\leq C_{w},X\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\} with ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, Σ=𝔼​ϕ​(X)​ϕ⊤​(X)\Sigma=\mathbb{E}\phi(X)\phi^{\top}(X). It guarantees ‖hw‖L2≤Cw​λmax​(Σ)\|h_{w}\|_{L_{2}}\leq C_{w}\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}. Covering a dd-dimensional ball of radius RR requires at most (C​R/ϵ)d(CR/\epsilon)^{d} points, thus J2≲d​λmax​(Σ)J_{2}\lesssim\sqrt{d}\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}.

Thus the uniform deviation decays as Op(N−1/2)O_{p}(N^{-1/2}). To ensure the empirical weak-learner edge approximates its population counterpart, we assume a variance floor, i.e., PN​(h(b))2>cℋaud2>0P_{N}(h^{(b)})^{2}>c_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}^{2}>0, to make passage from empirical to population more clear. Then we have

Lemma 15

Suppose ℋaud\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}} and ℋaud2\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2} are VC-classes with finite VC dimensions V⁡(ℋaud)V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}) and V⁡(ℋaud2)V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}^{2}), and there exists a variance floor for h(b)h^{(b)} along the boosting path, i.e., ‖h(b)‖L2​(ℙN)>cℋaud2>0\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N})}>c_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}^{2}>0, then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, if the sample size satisfies

Therefore, this result recovers the conclusions of earlier work Kim et al. (2019); Kim et al. (2022); Deng et al. (2023) while removing the restrictive uniform boundedness assumption. The variance floor condition is not overly stringent: we do not expect a degenerate case where h(b)(Xi)=0,i=1,…,Nh^{(b)}(X_{i})=0,i=1,\dots,N, since this would imply PN​h(b)​g=0P_{N}h^{(b)}g=0 and by convention we treat 0/0=00/0=0. The variance floor can always be ensured by normalization h~(b)=h(b)/‖h(b)‖L2​(ℙN)\widetilde{h}^{(b)}=h^{(b)}/\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N})}, or by incoporating a small stabilizing constant cℋaudc_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}} in the denominator of the violation statistic Δ~=PN​g(b)​h/(‖h‖L2​(ℙN)∧cℋaud)\widetilde{\Delta}=P_{N}g^{(b)}h/(\|h\|_{L_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N})}\wedge c_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}). In the latter case, one obtains

|⟨h(b),g(b)⟩|‖h(b)‖L2≥|⟨h(b),g(b)⟩|‖h(b)‖L2∧cℋaud>α−|(PN−P)​g(b)​h(b)|cℋaud.\frac{|\langle h^{(b)},g^{(b)}\rangle|}{\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}}\geq\frac{|\langle h^{(b)},g^{(b)}\rangle|}{\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}\wedge c_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}}>\alpha-\frac{|(P_{N}-P)g^{(b)}h^{(b)}|}{c_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}}.

The above argument subsumes the uniformly bounded settings frequently assumed in prior analyses, where ‖h‖∞≤Cℋaud\|h\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}; such a condition allows one to obtain bounds using classical concentration techniques like McDiarmid’s inequality or Hoeffding-type arguments for simpler concentration bounds. Our analysis, by contrast, accommodates more general auditor classes.

When data are limited, it is acceptable to evaluate the violation statistics (2) directly on the calibration set–an approach analogous to that in conformal inference (Romano et al., 2020a; Romano et al., 2020b; Candès et al., 2023). Furthermore, if algorithm halts after a finite number of steps BB, and one desires joint guarantee across all iterations with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the per-iteration probability should be set to 1−δ/B1-\delta/B. This adjustment leads to sample size requirement N=Ω⁡(V⁡(ℋaud)+log⁡(B/δ)α2)N=\Omega(\tfrac{V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})+\log(B/\delta)}{\alpha^{2}}).

Appendix D Special cases of multicalibration boosting

D.1 BatchGCP

Algorithm 1 of Jung et al. (2022), referred to as BatchGCP, aims to enforce group-wise coverage without calibration.

h(0)​(X)\displaystyle h^{(0)}(X) =𝒜(Ξ;(f(0)(Xi),Yi):Xi∈Ξ)\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}(\Xi;(f^{(0)}(X_{i}),Y_{i}):X_{i}\in\Xi)
≈arg​minh∈ℋaud⁡𝔼​[L⁡(Y,f(0)​(X)−h⁡(X))],\displaystyle\approx\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}\mathbb{E}[L(Y,f^{(0)}(X)-h(X))],

where there is a single global bucket Ξ\Xi and ℋaud={∑G∈𝒢βG𝟏{X∈G}:G∈𝒢}.\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\left\{\sum_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\beta_{G}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}:G\in\mathcal{G}\right\}. The updated predictor is then f~​(X)=f(0)​(X)−h(0)​(X)\widetilde{f}(X)=f^{(0)}(X)-h^{(0)}(X), which corresponds to a one-shot boosting refinement.

D.2 BatchMVP

We next show that Algorithm 2 of (Jung et al., 2022), MultiMVP, is a concrete instantiation of the generalized multicalibration boosting framework (Algorithm 1). Let fτ(0)​(X)f_{\tau}^{(0)}(X) be a pre-trined conditional quantile predictor at level τ\tau. Each prediction is first discretized onto an equally spaced grid,

qτ(0)​(X)=arg​minv∈[1/L]⁡|v−fτ(0)​(X)|,[1L]={0,1L,2L,…,1},q_{\tau}^{(0)}(X)=\argmin_{v\in[1/L]}|v-f_{\tau}^{(0)}(X)|,\quad[\tfrac{1}{L}]=\left\{0,\tfrac{1}{L},\tfrac{2}{L},\ldots,1\right\},

producing a snapped quantile estimate taking one of L+1L+1 discrete values. Define covariate-prediction buckets

SG,l={X∈G,qτ(b)(X)=vl},G∈𝒢,vl=lL,l=0,1,…,L.S_{G,l}=\{X\in G,q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X)=v_{l}\},\quad G\in\mathcal{G},v_{l}=\frac{l}{L},l=0,1,\ldots,L.

At iteration bb, the auditing step learns piecewise-constant function within

ℋaud={βG,l𝟏{X∈G}𝟏{qτ(b)=vl}:G∈𝒢,vl=[1/L]},\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}=\{\beta_{G,l}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}{\mathbf{1}}\{q_{\tau}^{(b)}=v_{l}\}:G\in\mathcal{G},v_{l}=[1/L]\},

which correspond to group-wise constant corrections over bucket SG,lS_{G,l}. That is, for each pair (G,vl)(G,v_{l}), the auditor fits

β^G,l𝟏{X∈G}𝟏{qτ(b)=vl}←𝒜(Ξ;{(Yi,qτ(b)(Xi)):Xi∈G,qτ(b)(Xi)=vl}),\widehat{\beta}_{G,l}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G\}{\mathbf{1}}\{q_{\tau}^{(b)}=v_{l}\}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(\Xi;\{(Y_{i},q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X_{i})):X_{i}\in G,q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X_{i})=v_{l}\}),

which amounts to regressing the subgradient

𝟏{Yi≤qτ(b)}−τ,Xi∈G,qτ(b)(Xi)=vl.{\mathbf{1}}\{Y_{i}\leq q_{\tau}^{(b)}\}-\tau,\quad X_{i}\in G,q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X_{i})=v_{l}.

The constant fit for each bucket therefore equals

β^G,l=∑SG,l𝟏{Yi≤vl}#​SG,l−τ, since ​qτ(b)​(Xi)=vl.\widehat{\beta}_{G,l}=\frac{\sum_{S_{G,l}}{\mathbf{1}}\{Y_{i}\leq v_{l}\}}{\#S_{G,l}}-\tau,\quad\text{ since }q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X_{i})=v_{l}.

As in Jung et al. (2022), the same data are used for both calibration and validation (Ξ=V)(\Xi=V), a standard practice in boosting. We do not make a distinction here.

The evaluation step then chooses

h(b)(X)=β^G∗,vl∗𝟏{X∈G∗}𝟏{qτ(b)(X)=vl∗},h^{(b)}(X)=\widehat{\beta}_{G^{*},v_{l}^{*}}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G^{*}\}{\mathbf{1}}\{q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X)=v_{l^{*}}\},

where (G∗,l∗)(G^{*},l^{*}) is the most violated bucket:

SG∗,l∗\displaystyle S_{G^{*},l^{*}} =arg​maxG,l⁡#​SG,l#​V​(∑SG,l𝟏{Yi≤vl}#​SG,l−τ)2\displaystyle=\argmax_{G,l}\frac{\#S_{G,l}}{\#V}\left(\frac{\sum_{S_{G,l}}{\mathbf{1}}\{Y_{i}\leq v_{l}\}}{\#S_{G,l}}-\tau\right)^{2}
≈arg​maxG,l⁡ℙ​(SG,l)​(τ−ℙ⁡(Y≤vl|qτ(b)​(X)=vl,X∈G))2.\displaystyle\approx\argmax_{G,l}\mathbb{P}(S_{G,l})\left(\tau-\mathbb{P}(Y\leq v_{l}|q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X)=v_{l},X\in G)\right)^{2}.

The selection rule exactly matches that of Algorithm 2 in Jung et al. (2022).

In their implementation, Jung et al. (2022) update the predictor by adding a small shift δ(b)\delta^{(b)} that re-aligns the empirical coverage:

δ(b)=arg​minδ∈[1/L]⁡|∑SG∗,l∗𝟏{Yi≤qτ(b)(Xi)+δ}#​SG∗,l∗−τ|.\delta^{(b)}=\argmin_{\delta\in[1/L]}\left|\frac{\sum_{S_{G^{*},l^{*}}}{\mathbf{1}}\{Y_{i}\leq q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X_{i})+\delta\}}{\#S_{G^{*},l^{*}}}-\tau\right|.

The quantile predictor is then updated as

qτ(b+1)(X)=qτ(b)(X)+δ(b)𝟏{X∈SG∗,l∗}.q_{\tau}^{(b+1)}(X)=q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X)+\delta^{(b)}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in S_{G^{*},l^{*}}\}.

This is equivalent to the boosting-style update

qτ(b+1)=qτ(b)(X)−η(b)(∑SG∗,l∗𝟏{Yi≤qτ(b)(Xi)}#​SG∗,l∗−τ)𝟏{X∈SG∗,l∗},q_{\tau}^{(b+1)}=q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X)-\eta^{(b)}\left(\tfrac{\sum_{S_{G^{*},l^{*}}}{\mathbf{1}}\{Y_{i}\leq q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X_{i})\}}{\#S_{G^{*},l^{*}}}-\tau\right){\mathbf{1}}\{X\in S_{G^{*},l^{*}}\},

with step size η(b)\eta^{(b)} chosen so that η(b)​β^G∗,l∗=δ(b)\eta^{(b)}\widehat{\beta}_{G^{*},l^{*}}=\delta^{(b)}.

Under this formulation, the learned predictor belongs to ℱ\mathcal{F}, which is the closure of class

{∑j=0kηjβGj,vlj𝟏{X∈Gj,qτ(b)(X)∈vlj}:Gj∈𝒢,vlj∈[1L],k∈ℕ}.\left\{\sum_{j=0}^{k}\eta_{j}\beta_{G_{j},v_{l_{j}}}{\mathbf{1}}\{X\in G_{j},q_{\tau}^{(b)}(X)\in v_{l_{j}}\}:G_{j}\in\mathcal{G},v_{l_{j}}\in[\tfrac{1}{L}],k\in\mathbb{N}\right\}.

To guarantee finite-sample multicalibration for a predictor obtained after finitely many updates, one may restrict attention to functions in ℱ\mathcal{F} with bounded L2L_{2} norm.

Appendix E Miscellaneuous

E.1 General convex but non-cLc_{L}-smooth loss

When ℒ\mathcal{L} is convex but not cLc_{L}-smooth, the faster O⁡(B−1)O(B^{-1}) and geometric rates of Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 are generally unavailable. In that case, we only guarantee the rate O(B−1/2)O(B^{-1/2}).

Theorem 16 (Convex, non-smooth loss)

Assume Conditions 1-4, and let OO be closed and convex. Suppose the MCBoost iterates satisfy f(b+1)=𝒫O​(f(b)−η(b)​h(b)),f^{(b+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{O}\bigl(f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)}\bigr), and for each bb, ‖h(b)−g(b)‖∗≤ε(b).\|h^{(b)}-g^{(b)}\|_{*}\leq\varepsilon^{(b)}. Let Δb:=ℒ⁡(f(b))−ℒ⁡(f(∞))\Delta_{b}:=\mathcal{L}(f^{(b)})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)}). Then, for any B≥1B\geq 1,

2​∑b=0B−1η(b)​Δb≤R2+Cℋaud2​∑b=0B−1η(b)​2+2​R​∑b=0B−1η(b)​ε(b).2\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}\Delta_{b}\leq R^{2}+C_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}^{2}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)2}+2R\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}\varepsilon^{(b)}. (17)

In particular, if η(b)≡η\eta^{(b)}\equiv\eta, then

min0≤b<B⁡Δb≤1B​∑b=0B−1Δb≤R22​η​B+η​Cℋaud22+RB​∑b=0B−1ε(b).\min_{0\leq b<B}\Delta_{b}\leq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\Delta_{b}\leq\frac{R^{2}}{2\eta B}+\frac{\eta C_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}^{2}}{2}+\frac{R}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\varepsilon^{(b)}.

Choosing η=R/(Cℋaud​B)\eta=R/(C_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}\sqrt{B}) gives

min0≤b<B⁡Δb≤1B​∑b=0B−1Δb≤R​CℋaudB+RB​∑b=0B−1ε(b).\min_{0\leq b<B}\Delta_{b}\leq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\Delta_{b}\leq\frac{RC_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}}{\sqrt{B}}+\frac{R}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\varepsilon^{(b)}.

Moreover, for the averaged iterate f¯B=B−1​∑b=0B−1f(b)\bar{f}_{B}=B^{-1}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}f^{(b)},

ℒ⁡(f¯B)−ℒ⁡(f(∞))≤R​CℋaudB+RB​∑b=0B−1ε(b)=O⁡(1/B),\mathcal{L}(\bar{f}_{B})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\leq\frac{RC_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}}}}{\sqrt{B}}+\frac{R}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\varepsilon^{(b)}=O(1/\sqrt{B}),

Proof Since 𝒫O\mathcal{P}_{O} is nonexpansive,

‖f(b+1)−f(∞)‖L22≤‖f(b)−η(b)​h(b)−f(∞)‖L22.\|f^{(b+1)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}\leq\|f^{(b)}-\eta^{(b)}h^{(b)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}.

≤‖f(b)−f(∞)‖L22−‖f(b+1)−f(∞)‖L22+η(b)​2​‖h(b)‖L22+2​η(b)​R​ε(b)\displaystyle\leq\|f^{(b)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}-\|f^{(b+1)}-f^{(\infty)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}+\eta^{(b)2}\|h^{(b)}\|_{L_{2}}^{2}+2\eta^{(b)}R\varepsilon^{(b)}

ℒ⁡(f¯B)−ℒ⁡(f(∞))≤1B​∑b=0B−1Δb,\mathcal{L}(\bar{f}_{B})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})\leq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\Delta_{b},

Remark 7 (Unknown horizon and diminishing step size)

If the horizon BB is unknown in advance, one may use a diminishing step size η(b)≍(b+1)−1/2\eta^{(b)}\asymp(b+1)^{-1/2}. Then

∑b=0B−1η(b)≍B,∑b=0B−1η(b)​2≍log⁡B,\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}\asymp\sqrt{B},\qquad\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)2}\asymp\log B,

and (17) yields

∑b=0B−1η(b)​Δb∑b=0B−1η(b)≲log⁡BB+R​∑b=0B−1η(b)​ε(b)∑b=0B−1η(b).\frac{\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}\Delta_{b}}{\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}}\lesssim\frac{\log B}{\sqrt{B}}+\frac{R\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}\varepsilon^{(b)}}{\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}}.

Hence, if ∑b=0B−1η(b)​ε(b)=o⁡(log⁡B)\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}\varepsilon^{(b)}=o(\log B), the weighted average iterate

f¯B=∑b=0B−1η(b)​f(b)∑b=0B−1η(b)\bar{f}_{B}=\frac{\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}f^{(b)}}{\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\eta^{(b)}}

achieves

ℒ⁡(f¯B)−ℒ⁡(f(∞))=O⁡(log⁡BB).\mathcal{L}(\bar{f}_{B})-\mathcal{L}(f^{(\infty)})=O\!\left(\frac{\log B}{\sqrt{B}}\right).

Thus, in the non-smooth convex setting, one needs B=O⁡(α−2)B=O(\alpha^{-2}) iterations to reach excess risk of order α\alpha, up to the auditing approximation term. If this population bound is combined with the same VC-type concentration argument used in Proposition 7, the natural sample-size scale remains

N=Ω⁡(log⁡(B/δ)+V⁡(ℋaud)α2).N=\Omega\!\left(\frac{\log(B/\delta)+V(\mathcal{H}_{\text{aud}})}{\alpha^{2}}\right).
Classification losses.

In classification, logistic and exponential losses are common examples. It is useful to record their score functions explicitly.

Appendix F Additional numerical results

F.1 Disregarding the group splitting and group features

F.2 Excess risk and interaction between initial predictors and auditors

The phenomena in the main numerical finding are also reflected in the excess risk curves based on MSE. When no group partition is used (|𝒢|=1|\mathcal{G}|=1), constant refinement yields negligible improvement in MSE. When group structure is introduced (|𝒢|=4|\mathcal{G}|=4), constant refinement can reduce the MSE of the initial random forest estimator regardless of whether the categorical features X(d)X^{(d)} are explicitly included in MCBoost. However, it improves the MSE of the initial linear model only if X(d)X^{(d)} covariates are not taken into account. With these variables included, the linear model already satisfies the corresponding moment conditions, leaving little room for further correction by a constant auditor. This highlights the interaction between the initial predictor and the auditor class: the effectiveness of post-processing depends on the extent to which the auditor introduces new directions not already captured by the initial model.

F.3 Structural groups and weighted shifts under covariate shift

In Section 4.2, we evaluate MCBoost beyond prespecified demographic groups by using structural subgroups and weighted shifts constructed from standardized continuous covariates Z=(Z1,Z2)Z=(Z_{1},Z_{2}), where ZjZ_{j} is obtained by zz-scoring the corresponding component of X(c)X^{(c)} using the reference sample. These targets are designed to probe interaction-dominated regions, high-curvature regions, and localized departures from the source distribution. Unless otherwise stated, all thresholds are computed from the sample after standardization.

We consider the following representative structural subgroups:

  • •

    Interaction region (interaction_reg): observations for which the interaction term Z1​Z2Z_{1}Z_{2} is unusually large in magnitude, corresponding to the upper or lower tail of the interaction score.

  • •

    interaction_neg (interaction_neg): observations with Z1​Z2≤q0.20​(Z1​Z2)Z_{1}Z_{2}\leq q_{0.20}(Z_{1}Z_{2}).

  • •

    Hard region (hard_region): observations with a large composite difficulty score

    d⁡(Z)=0.5​|Z1|+0.3​Z22+0.2​|Z1​Z2|d(Z)=0.5|Z_{1}|+0.3Z_{2}^{2}+0.2|Z_{1}Z_{2}|

    satisfying d⁡(Z)≥q0.85​(d⁡(Z))d(Z)\geq q_{0.85}(d(Z)).

We also consider the following weighted shifts. In each case, we form raw weights, clip them to the interval [0.1,10][0.1,10], and renormalize them to have empirical mean 11:

  • •

    Curvature tilt (curvature_tilt): w⁡(X)∝exp⁡(0.4​Z22)w(X)\propto\exp(0.4Z_{2}^{2}).

  • •

    Hard mixed tilt (hard_mixed_tilt):

    w⁡(X)∝exp⁡(0.30​|Z1|+0.25​Z22+0.25​Z1​Z2+0.25​X6+0.25​X7).w(X)\propto\exp\big(0.30|Z_{1}|+0.25Z_{2}^{2}+0.25Z_{1}Z_{2}+0.25X_{6}+0.25X_{7}\big).
  • •

    Local bump (local_bump): a Gaussian bump centered at (1.2,−1.0)(1.2,-1.0) in the (Z1,Z2)(Z_{1},Z_{2}) plane with bandwidth 0.80.8, namely

    w⁡(X)∝exp⁡(−(Z1−1.2)2+(Z2+1.0)22×0.82).w(X)\propto\exp\left(-\frac{(Z_{1}-1.2)^{2}+(Z_{2}+1.0)^{2}}{2\times 0.8^{2}}\right).
